response: Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have become an essential source of data for researchers and practitioners who aim to understand the behavior, sentiment, and emotions of large populations. The ever-growing availability of social media data has led to a surge in the development of various models for predicting community-level outcomes based on the aggregated text from social media posts. Nowcasting, in particular, has gained significant attention due to its ability to provide unobtrusive and near real-time predictions of potential outcomes. A common approach to nowcasting relies on aggregating all social media posts without consideration for individual users, which assumes that aggregated data reflects the collective behavior of the community. However, research has shown that aggregating data without regard to users may lead to inaccurate or biased estimates of the population's behavior, attitudes, and emotions. Consequently, an increasing number of researchers and practitioners have started to explore alternative approaches to nowcasting that focus on individual users and their social connections. This shift towards user-level analysis is driven by the understanding that each user contributes distinctly to the aggregated data, which can lead to improved accuracy and reduced bias in predictions. By examining the language aggregated by user, researchers can identify patterns, trends, and relevant correlations that may be hidden when analyzing aggregated data. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method for building community-level models using Twitter language aggregated by user. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach through results on four different U.S. county-level tasks, spanning demographic, health, and psychological outcomes. Our experiments show large and consistent improvements in prediction accuracies over the standard approach of aggregating all tweets. For instance, in terms of median income prediction, our results show a significant increase from a Pearson r value of 0.73 to 0.82. Similarly, for life satisfaction prediction, our approach leads to an improvement from a Pearson r value of 0.37 to 0.47. Our research contributes to the growing body of literature that highlights the importance of considering individual users in social media analysis. By leveraging user-level data, we can gain deeper insights into the collective behavior of social media users, ultimately leading to more accurate predictions of community-level outcomes. To facilitate further research, we provide access to our aggregated and anonymized community-level data, derived from 37 billion tweets, with over 1 billion of which were mapped to counties. Our data is publicly available for research purposes, enabling others to build upon our findings and explore the benefits of user-level aggregation in social media nowcasting. However, code-switching poses significant challenges to natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as part-of-speech (POS) tagging, where the model struggles to identify the language of the input text. This issue is further exacerbated when the input text contains transliteration, where words from one language are represented using the script of another language (e.g., English words written in Hindi script). Despite the prevalence of code-switching, NLP models often rely on explicit language identification (ELI) to determine the language of the input text, which is not only error-prone but also requires large amounts of labeled data for different languages. In contrast, this paper proposes an innovative approach to addressing the challenges of code-switching by developing a novel model architecture that can be trained and deployed without requiring explicit language identification. Our approach, which we call "inference-driven, multi-language POS tagging," leverages the flexibility of neural network architectures to jointly maintain separate word representations for each possible language or script. This design enables our model to generalize across different languages and scripts, allowing it to make accurate POS tagging decisions without requiring explicit language identification. Our model is based on the idea of representational independence, where each language or script is treated as a separate entity with its own internal representation. This is achieved by introducing a novel module, called the "languageattention mechanism," which allows the model to dynamically attend to the relevant language or script based on the input text. By maintaining separate representations for each language or script, our model can learn to identify the language or script of the input text without requiring explicit language identification. response: Image retrieval models have been a cornerstone of computer vision research for decades, with applications ranging from content-based image retrieval to object recognition. Conventional image retrieval models represent images as a bag-of-terms, where each image is reduced to a set of visual features or descriptors, typically extracted from predefined regions or directly from the entire image. These representations are particularly well-suited for matching images based on the presence or absence of certain features. However, for certain types of queries, a more nuanced understanding of how image regions relate to each other is necessary. For instance, imagine a user searching for images of people performing specific actions, such as someone cooking in a kitchen. While a bag-of-terms representation might return images of people holding kitchen utensils, it will struggle to distinguish between images of people who are simply interacting with objects versus those who are actively engaging in the activity. Incorporating spatial information about the relationships between image regions is crucial for capturing the complexities of human activity understanding in image retrieval. Visual Dependency Representations (VDRs) aim to address this by providing a structured representation of image regions, which captures their syntactic relationships to one another. In a VDR, an image is represented as a directed graph, where nodes are image regions, and edges encode the dependency relationships between these regions. For example, in an image of a person stirring a pot, the person node might depend on the stirring motion node, which in turn depends on the pot node, and so on. This high-level representation of image structure enables distinguishing between images where objects only co-occur from images where they interact or are manipulated by the subject. In this paper, we investigate the utility of VDRs for improving image retrieval performance on query-by-example tasks, where a user provides an example image and seeks similar images in a database. Specifically, we conduct a thorough evaluation of VDRs on the Stanford-Action dataset, a benchmark collection of images depicting 8 action categories. In an end-to-end histogram comparison and query-by-example experiment, we compare the performance of VDRs against a more traditional bag-of-terms baseline. Our results demonstrate that VDRs are a viable alternative to bag-of-terms representations, yielding a 8.8% relative improvement in MAP and 8.6% relative improvement in Precision@10. Our findings provide evidence that structured representations of image regions, such as those captured by VDRs, can serve as a valuable complement to more traditional feature-based retrieval approaches. Furthermore, we anticipate that VDRs may have wider applicability in the context of human activity understanding, object manipulation, and interaction understanding. response: Discourse parsing is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), aiming to hierarchically identify the discourse relations within a text and assign them to a specific scope. Among various discourse parsing frameworks, the Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST)-style document-level discourse parsing has drawn significant attention in recent years due to its ability to capture group-level relationships and use discourse relations to understand the global meaning of a text. However, RST-style document-level discourse parsing remains a challenging task, mainly due to the complex nature of discourse relations, the large number of possible discourse structures, and the need to capture the interactions between distant elements in the text. Despite the advancements in NLP, the deep learning-based approaches for RST-style document-level discourse parsing have rarely been thoroughly studied. The lack of efficient deep learning models for this task makes manual feature engineering a conventional method to achieve acceptable performance, leading to the proliferation of complex and cumbersome feature engineering pipelines. In this context, developing a deep learning model that can directly learn useful representations of discourse structures and relations from raw text data without extensive manual feature engineering is highly desirable. Towards this goal, we propose a novel attention-based hierarchical neural network (AHNN) for RST-style document-level discourse parsing. In particular, we design a tensor-based transformation function to model the complicated feature interactions, which is differentiable and can be solved via backpropagation. Our model is able to dynamically focus on relevant parts of the text and learn hierarchical representations that capture the discourse relations and their scopes. Extensive experiments on the discourse parsed data demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable or even better performance than the contemporary state-of-the-art systems with limited manual feature engineering, while significantly improving the processing efficiency. In addition, we provide an in-depth analysis of our proposed model, including itsarchitecture, the tensor-based transformation function, and the attention mechanism. Our results highlight the effectiveness of the deep learning-based approach for RST-style document-level discourse parsing and reveal an alternative to the conventional manual feature engineering methods. By leveraging the AHNN and tensor-based transformation function, we are able to directly learn from raw text data and provide interpretable internal representations that contribute to the discourse understanding. These results offer a fruitful foundation for future research on discourse parsing and related NLP applications. Our proposed model is also envisioned to be more adaptable and extendable to other NLP tasks, which require modeling complex hierarchical relationships. Rather, the reader actively engages with the text, constructing a mental representation that conveys the author's intended message. This process, whereby the reader infers and elaborates upon the meaning of a text, is often referred to as an "inferential" or "constructionist" view of comprehension (Millis and Stahl, 2006). From this perspective, the goal of reading is not just to recognize individual words, but to create a rich, coherent picture of the world being described. This picture, or "scene," constitutes the reader's understanding of the text, and can be used to inform new inferences and answers to questions that go beyond the specific content of the text (Grafton, 2009). When we encounter new information, whether through text, speech, or observation, we automatically begin to construct a mental representation of the scene, using our prior knowledge and experience to fill in gaps and make sense of what we encounter (Tversky, 1975). This process is especially critical for understanding certain types of texts, such as narratives, where the reader must piece together a sequence of events and characters to form a coherent picture of the story (Zwaan, 1993). response: Generating a coherent and concise summary from a long piece of text is an essential task in natural language processing, with applications in information retrieval, question answering, and text summarization. Traditional summarization methods, such as extractive and abstractive summarization, have been well-studied, but they often fail to capture the coherence of the input text (Liu et al., 2009). Most existing summarization methods aim to select the most relevant sentences from the source document and order them to form a summary. However, this process can result in a summary that is not coherent with the original document. Coherence is particularly important in summarization, as it can help readers to quickly understand the main points of the document and grasp the underlying relationships between the different ideas (Radev and McKeown, 2003). Many approaches to modeling coherence in summarization rely on the use of graph-based models, such as the Topic-Sentiment Graph (Chen et al., 2011), or on the exploitation of more structured representations of text, such as topic modeling (Mihalcea and Csomai, 2007). In the graph-based approach, sentences are integrated into a graph, and the coherence of a sentence is based on the connectivity with the previous sentences. For certain type of texts such as news articles, sentences can be connected by their similar topics, entities, or time. However, this way of deciding the coherence might not apply to all types of documents. In addition, the results of these methods are based solely on the assignment of features and weights, and the relationships between the sentences are hard to visualize and interpret. To address this challenge, a Hidden Semi-Markov Model (HSMM) has been popularized in the applications of natural language processing, such as parsing, dialogue, and sequence labeling tasks, due to its effectiveness in modeling sequential data with variable-length segments (Russell and Norvig, 2009). In this study, we propose a novel summarization method based on HSMM, which can naturally model the relationship between the sentence succession and the coherence of the summary. Our method optimizes the selection of sentences to form the summary with the objective of maximizing the coherence among the selected sentences, which is subject to a knapsack constraint that limits the total summary length (Keller and Wiegand, 2015). This optimization process allows us to systematically evaluate the contributions of different sentences to the coherence of the summary. Our model can also incorporate sentence compression into the summarization process, following the approach taken by (Wang et al., 2018) where predefined slots are used to capture the basic semantic structures related to text compression. response: Code generation is a challenging task that has garnered significant interest from the natural language processing (NLP) and software engineering communities. With the rising tide of software applications, the importance of automated code generation is becoming increasingly evident. Traditionally, code generation is performed using general-purpose tools that aim to produce code directly from specifications or natural language descriptions. While these tools have shown impressive results in various tasks, they fall short in providing code that is tailored to the specific context of a program. In reality, source code is rarely written in isolation. It heavily depends on the programmatic context, which includes the class that the code would reside in. This context contains essential information about the expected behavior of the program, including the interfaces, data structures, and constraints that the code will interact with. Unfortunately, this context is often overlooked in code generation tasks, resulting in general-purpose code that may not align with the specific requirements of a program. To study this phenomenon, we introduce the task of generating class member functions given English documentation and the programmatic context provided by the rest of the class. This task poses several challenges. First, the desired code can vary greatly depending on the functionality the class provides. For example, a sort function may or may not be available when we are asked to "return the smallest element" in a particular member variable list. Second, the programmatic context may contain complex relationships between different classes, methods, and variables, which need to be accurately captured in the generated code. To address these challenges, we introduce CONCODE, a new large dataset with over 100,000 examples consisting of Java classes from online code repositories. Each example in the dataset contains the following: a Java class with its member variables and functions, an English documentation describing the behavior of a particular member function, and the desired code for that function. We also develop a new encoder-decoder architecture that models the interaction between the method documentation and the class environment. Our architecture is based on the transformer model (Vaswani et al., 2017), which we adapt to encode the programmatic context and the method documentation separately. The encoder part of the model takes the Java class and the method documentation as input and generates a joint representation that captures their relationship. The decoder part generates the code for the member function based on this joint representation. We also propose several innovations to the transformer model, including attention mechanisms that allow the model to focus on specific parts of the code and the documentation. We evaluate our model on the CONCODE dataset and show that it achieves state-of-the-art results in several tasks, including code generation and debugging. We also present a detailed error analysis suggesting that there is significant room for future work on this task, including better handling of complex relationships between classes and methods, and improved handling of abstract concepts and domain knowledge. Overall, our work demonstrates that modeling the programmatic context is a crucial step in generating accurate and useful code, and it provides a foundation for future research in this area. response: Statistical machine translation (SMT) is a popular approach to natural language translation. It uses n-gram language models to predict the next word in a sentence given the context of previous words. Among various language models, continuous-space language models (CSLMs) have recently gained significant attention for their state-of-the-art performance in language modeling tasks (Mikolov et al., 2010b; Mikolov et al., 2011). CSLMs are neural network models that learn to represent the probability distribution over a vocabulary using dense vectors. The learned vectors, also known as word embeddings, have exhibited impressive capabilities in language modeling tasks, such as language modeling perplexity and automatic speech recognition. Despite their success, CSLMs are not typically used in the first pass decoding of SMT systems. The main reason for this is that the computation of the language model probabilities, which is typically performed at runtime, is slower than the computation of n-gram model probabilities, which are usually precomputed and stored in memory. One possible solution to this problem is to precompute and store the CSLM probabilities at training time, similar to what is done in the case of traditional n-gram language models. However, as pointed out in (Li et al., 2005), computing the CSLM probabilities at training time is very time-consuming. In fact, the time complexity is in the order of O(ntv), where n is the number of training examples, t is the number of tokens in the vocabulary, and v is the dimensionality of the space. This makes it impractical to store the precomputed CSLM probabilities. On the other hand, n-gram language models (NLMMs), which are commonly used in SMT, are typically trained and stored offline. Their probability computation has a linear time complexity, making it very efficient. However, n-gram language models suffer from the problem of data sparsity, where a large number of rare or unseen events are ignored. To address this problem, back-off n-gram language models (BNLMs) are trained as a hierarchical model (Jelinek et al., 1977). They are trained to predict a higher-order language model probability by backing off from a lower-order alternative when encountering an unseen sequence of words. However, the training of a BNLM from scratch is computationally expensive. By converting a CSLM into a BNLM, we can leverage the computation efficiency of the n-gram language model while keeping the interpretability and robustness of the neural network based language model. response: The Transformer model, proposed by Vaswani et al. in 2017, has achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of machine translation tasks due to its ability to handle long-range dependencies and provide parallelized computation. However, the original Transformer model still has limitations when dealing with discourse phenomena, such as coherence and anaphora resolution, where document-level context is crucial. This is mainly because the Transformer model typically focuses on one sentence at a time without considering potential relationships between sentences in a document. In this work, we extend the Transformer model by incorporating a new context encoder to represent document-level context, which can improve its performance in handling discourse phenomena. Traditional machine translation models, such as phrase-based and syntax-based models, have taken advantage of the document-level context to capture more nuances of the original text, especially for languages with complex discourse structures. However, these models often ignore the subtlety of semantic relationships and the contextualization of co-references, which can significantly affect the accuracy of machine translation. The Transformer model overcomes some of these limitations by representing the input sequence as a sequence of vectors and using self-attention to compute the representation of each token by considering the entire input sequence. However, as pointed out by Tran et al. (2019), the self-attention mechanism in the original Transformer model often relies too heavily on local information, failing to capture the relationships between non-adjacent sentences in a document. In such cases, the model tends to overlook essential discourse phenomena, resulting in suboptimal translation quality. This motivated our investigation into how to provide the Transformer model with a better awareness of document-level context. To this end, we present a new context encoder that captures the essence of document-level context and incorporates it into the original Transformer encoder and decoder. The key idea is to represent the entire document as a single, flattened sequence of tokens, rather than a sequence of individual sentences, allowing the self-attention mechanism to consider the entire document when computing the representation of each token. By doing so, we enable the Transformer model to capture the relationships between non-adjacent sentences, potentially improving its performance in handling discourse phenomena. This pre-training step allows the model to learn how to capture the relationships between sentences within a document. In the second step, the "document-level fine-tuning" step, we further refine the pre-trained model using the limited document-level parallel corpora. By doing so, we enable the model to adapt to the document-level context and capture more nuanced discourse phenomena. response: Relation extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, question answering, and text summarization (Mintz et al., 2009; Riedel et al., 2010). The goal of relation extraction is to identify entities and their relationships in unstructured text, such as "John Smith is the CEO of XYZ Corporation". This task is challenging due to the complexity and ambiguity of natural language, as well as the vast number of possible relations. To address these challenges, numerous approaches have been proposed, including dictionary-based methods (Ji and Grishman, 2008), kernel methods (Cao et al., 2010), distant supervision-based methods (Mintz et al., 2009) and deep learning-based methods (Zeng et al., 2014). Among these methods, distant supervision, which relies on existing knowledge graphs, has emerged as a popular approach for relation extraction (Mintz et al., 2009). The key idea of distant supervision-based methods is to leverage existing knowledge graphs, such as Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008) and Wikidata (Vrandečić and Kraker, 2012), to automatically collect training data. With these data, the task of relation extraction becomes a classification problem: given a sentence, identify the relation between the entities mentioned in that sentence. Although distant supervision is effective in scaling relation extraction up to large-scale corpora, it inevitably suffers from the wrong labeling problem (Zeng et al., 2014). In other words, some entities in a sentence may not actually be related, but are labeled as a relation due to the noise in the knowledge graph. To address this issue, many efforts have been devoted to identifying valid instances from noisy data (Zeng et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Nguyen and Nguyen, 2017). However, most existing methods handle each relation in isolation, regardless of rich semantic correlations located in relation hierarchies (Alon et al., 2019). Relation hierarchies, such as RBox (Bao et al., 2017), provide a systematic way to organize relations, with more specific relations nested under more general ones. For instance, 'type of animal' is nested under 'living thing'. Incorporating this hierarchical information of relations may help to better identify valid instances from noisy data. A remarkable application of social media is in understanding how users form and change their opinions about a product, and how these opinions are influenced by their friends and social networks. The field of opinion formation has received considerable attention in recent years, particularly in computer science and data analysis communities. Prior studies on opinion formation have traditionally modeled opinions as discrete or continuous sentiment values without considering the underlying semantic information (Li et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2016). However, existing MT systems often struggle to handle names, which are a crucial component of many translations. Names can be properly or improperly translated, affecting the overall quality of the translation and potentially leading to misunderstandings or misidentifications. For instance, translating the name "Liu Bei" from Chinese to English as "Liu Pie" would not only be grammatically incorrect but also change the meaning of the original sentence. Similarly, translating "Liu Bei" as "Bobby Liu" changes the emotional connotation of the sentence. Previous work on name translation and word alignment often treats names as regular words in the sentence, and ignores the unique properties of names in terms of translation and alignment. However, in Chinese-English translation, the properties such as, translation rules, translation patterns and constraints should be well respected and modeled to conduct name translation effectively, especially for proper noun translation. In this paper, we propose a Name-aware Machine Translation (MT) approach which integrates name processing into the MT model, by jointly annotating parallel corpora, extracting name-aware translation grammar and rules, adding name phrase table, and implementing name translation driven decoding. In a social setting, speakers and listeners must cooperate in order to achieve a common goal, which is to effectively convey and understand information. This cooperation is governed by the cooperative principle proposed by Grice(Grice, 1975). According to Grice, speakers are expected to make only contributions that serve the evolving conversational goals. This principle is supported by four maxims: quality (be truthful), quantity (give a little more than necessary), relevance (stay on topic) and manner (avoid ambiguity). The Gricean approach to communication provides a fundamental framework for understanding and predicting how people communicate, both in natural language and in artificial systems. In this problem, the goal is to develop a method that can accurately translate natural language sentences into logical representations of their meaning. Traditionally, this task has been approached through the use of hand-crafted grammars and rule-based systems. With user questions being typically short and high-level semantic expressions, uncovering their underlying meaning can be very challenging. We propose an approach to this challenge by use of powerful semantic classifiers that are able to identify relevant features from the language input (Mitchell et al., 2003),along with incorporation of supervised clustering methods that are useful for extracting salient relationships between our classifier outputs. While there exist techniques for question retrieval (Yang et al., 2005) and question classification (Ravichandran and Hovy, 2002), little attention has been given to the task of clustering of questions into meaningful intent categories. SOC offers several potential advantages: by describing a pair of relevant relation along with class label that distinguishes them from other pairs and by considering how these unseen relationships are computed through applying appropriate models both explicitly and in real-time. Recent advances in paraphrase generation have mainly relied on the encoder-decoder framework, with the exception of some work on multi- task learning (Zhou et al., 2018) and post-processing techniques (Budzianowski et al., 2019). However, these models suffer from a major limitation: they tend to memorize the words and patterns in the training dataset instead of learning the meaning of the words. As a result, the generated sentences often lack semantic correctness and coherence, even if they are syntactically correct. In an attempt to address this issue, this paper proposes a novel approach to paraphrase generation, using a Word Embedding Attention Network (WEAN) that combines the strengths of encoder-decoders and neural word embeddings. Unlike traditional models that rely solely on pre-trained word embeddings, our proposed approach treats word embeddings as a query space and perform a sorting process that samples highly-ranked word relevant to the given source text upon each decoding step. They are typically implemented as n-gram models, where the probability of a word being emitted given its n-1 preceding words is estimated based on a large corpus of text. N-gram language models have several advantages over other models, including simplicity, effectiveness, and ease of implementation. However, as the size of the corpus increases, the size of the n-gram model also grows, leading to increased memory requirements and slower query times. This is because the model needs to store data for every possible n-gram in the corpus, which can result in a large number of entries. One way to mitigate this problem is to use more efficient data structures to represent the n-gram model. In general, a language model comprises three main components: the vocabulary, the n-gram table, and the arithmetic coder. The vocabulary is a set of unique words in the language, and the n-gram table stores the count of each n-gram in the corpus. The arithmetic coder is used to perform arithmetic coding and decoding of the linguistic entropy of the input data, and is driven by the n-gram table and the probability distributions it contains. Hash tables have been traditionally used to represent the n-gram table, as they allow for fast lookup and insertion operations. However, they can still consume a lot of memory, especially for large corpora. In this work, we explore an alternative data structure, the double-array, which has shown promising results in representing large-scale n-gram language models. The double-array is a sparse array data structure that uses two arrays, one for words and the other for word counts, to represent a dictionary. This data structure has been shown to be highly efficient in terms of memory usage and query speed. Moreover, it can handle large-scale dictionaries with tens of millions of entries. This approach reduces the model size by storing the probabilities of each word in the unused spaces of the vocabulary array. response: Machine translation is a challenging task that involves translating content from one language to another. The quality of machine translation is determined by the ability of the translation model to understand the context and nuances of the source language and then translate it accurately into the target language. One approach to machine translation is phrase-based translation, which is based on the idea that phrases in a sentence are often translated as a whole rather than individual words. However, phrase-based translation makes the phrasal independence assumption, which assumes that phrases are translated independently of their surrounding context. However, this assumption does not always hold, as phrases are often dependent on the context in which they occur. To overcome the limitations of phrase-based translation, various approaches have been proposed, including neural machine translation (NMT) models, which are based on the idea of modeling the entire sentence as a single sequence of word embeddings. One of the key challenges in NMT is handling out-of-vocabulary words, which are words that do not appear in the training data. To address this challenge, various methods have been proposed, including subword modeling and morphological segmentation. Despite their success, NMT models still have some limitations, such as the difficulty in handling long-range dependencies and the high computational cost of training large models. To address these limitations, researchers have proposed various variants of NMT models, including recurrent neural network (RNN) models and transformer models. In this paper, we propose a recurrent neural network-based tuple sequence model (RNNTSM) for machine translation. Our RNNTSM is designed to capture long-range dependencies by modeling tuples in a sentence as a sequence of word embeddings. Unlike traditional NMT models, our RNNTSM uses a tuple sequence model to capture the relationships between words in a sentence. response: Temporal information extraction is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), computer vision, and notably question answering (QA), with applications in diverse domains such as event detection, information retrieval, and surveillance. QA systems, in particular, rely heavily on temporal information to provide accurate and relevant answers to the query. Traditionally, temporal information extraction tasks have been addressed using rule-based approaches, hand-crafted dictionaries, or machine learning techniques (Damlakhi et al., 2013). However, with the advent of deep learning, especially Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architectures, many of the classical NLP tasks have observed significant improvements in terms of accuracy and efficiency (Collobert et al., 2011;Goller and Kuchler, 1996). Temporal information extraction, however, despite its importance, has remained a problem of considerable challenge due to the coarseness of existing annotations, the varied expression patterns of temporal relations, and the skewness in dataset distributions (Varlamis and Vazirgiannis, 2005).Central to the task of temporal information extraction is the identification of relevant temporal relations between entities within text, including relative time expression, disorder relation, previous/following relation, and document creation time relation. These relations can be categorized mainly into intra-sentence, crosssentence, and document creation time relations. Traditional machine learning based approaches, such as Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Conditional Random Field (CRF), have been successful in extracting specific types of relations but often require extensive feature engineering, computational resources, and time for model training (Zhou et al., 2003;Taskar et al., 2003). Deep learning models have demonstrated significant improvements over traditional machine learning techniques in various NLP tasks, such as language modeling (Sutskever et al., 2011), sentiment analysis (Sulic et al., 2005), and text classification (Kim, 2014). The LSTM-based architecture is particularly well-suited for temporal information extraction due to its adaptability in learning internal temporal structures and strengths in dealing with complex sequential data (Sundermeyer et al., 2010). However, current LSTM-based architectures for temporal information extraction suffer from limitations such as requirement of hand-crafted features, inefficient extraction of multi-span relations, ambiguity in returning relations (many relations may exist in the same document), and falling back based on diverse quality of annotators. The goal of event schema induction is to extract the key entities, events, and relationships that are involved in a given text or corpus, and to represent them in a structured and interpretable format. Event schema induction has wide range of potential applications in various domains, including information retrieval, question answering, text summarization, and text generation. Traditional event schema induction methods typically rely on manually designed and domain-specific features, such as part-of-speech tags, named entity recognition, and dependency parsing (Chambers and Zoubin, 2001;Gupta and Takeshi, 2013). However, these methods are often limited in their ability to capture the complexity and nuance of real-world events and entities. For example, previous studies have shown that head words, which are commonly used to represent entities, often lack in specificity and discriminativeness (McCarthy et al., 2015). An armed man, for instance, is a more informative and distinctive representation of an entity than just man. Recent studies have explored the use of probabilistic topic models to represent event schemas, which have been shown to be effective in capturing latent semantic relationships and structures in text data (Blei et al., 2003). However, most previous studies have focused on using head words alone to represent entities, and have ignored the valuable information that can be captured by other elements such as modifiers, adjuncts, and complements. Our study aims to bridge this gap by introducing a generative model that precisely represents entities using probabilistic topic distributions and accounts for the useful information contained in elements other than head words. We denote an event schema as a quadruple (T, e, R, l), where T is the topic distribution over an event's argument roles, e is the entity that fills an event's argument role, R is the relationship between entities in an event schema, and l is the location where the event takes place. We illustrate that the probabilistic topic distributions provide a more coherent representation of an event's argument roles and their relationships to entities, resulting in more accurate and more informative event schemas. Most importantly, our evaluations show that our generative model performs better than previous methods on the task of event schema induction, indicating the usefulness of incorporating additional information from elements other than head words through probabilistic topic distributions. response: Reported performance scores of a machine learning model often give a misleading view of its reliability and generalizability. A widely practiced evaluation scenario is to report a single performance score on a single evaluation set, where the performance score is obtained from a single run of a random initialisation of the models' weights (i.e., a single random execution). Due to the inherent randomness of the learning process of many popular neural network architectures (Arpit et al., 2017), a single score is heavily dependent on the selected random seed value, which can significantly affect the performance of the model (Japkowicz and Shah, 2011;Diffe, 1991). Consequently, comparing the performance of two different approaches based on a single score can be unfair, because the differences may be attributed not to the approaches themselves, but to the random initialisation. In fact, by randomly testing the performance over different runs, one will observe that often the top result drops significantly in the subsequent runs (Ninunload weekly, personal communication). This issue affects not only the comparison of different machine learning approaches, but also their perceived quality, since the performance is often used as a metric to judge the models quality and efficacy. A more realistic evaluation of a model's performance should be done over multiple executions to gather a certain level of confidence in the model's performance and to reduce the randomness effect (Châteauneuf et al., 2014). In the context of sequence tagging, such as named-entity recognition (NER), the performance differences can be substantial and although tiny changes in the evaluation metrics may appear to be irrelevant, they have real-world implications in terms of improving the performance of a model. However, examining multiple runs manually would rapidly become almost unbearable, so automated ways to distinguish and quantify these effects are needed. Therefore, in this paper, we investigate whether testing over random initialisations can be used to identify the optimal sequence tagging model. We investigate five common sequence tagging tasks and compare the performance histogram distributions of several network architectures, both in terms of their performance and their stability. One of our main questions is whether certain network architectures adapt better than others to the different executions. This concept has revolutionized Natural Language Processing (NLP) and is ubiquitous in current NLP applications, such as language modeling, sentiment analysis, question answering, and machine translation. Existing work on word embeddings focuses on group-level representations where a whole word is treated as a single unit, ignoring its internal structure. This is largely due to the fact that most languages exhibit a combinatorial property where words are composed of letters or alphabets, such as English. In contrast, Chinese is a logographic language where a word often consists of one or more Chinese characters, each of which carries rich semantic information. This intrinsic property of Chinese characters poses a unique challenge in learning effective representations of Chinese words. In other words, word-level embeddings are not sufficient to capture the nuances of Chinese language, and character-level representations often become essential. In this work, we investigate two novel character-enhanced Chinese character embedding models and their bigram extensions, which aim to inject the valuable information from character components into word-level representations. Unlike existing English word embeddings, our models take into account the inherent semantic cues hidden within Chinese characters and their compositions. By learning compact yet informative character embeddings, we aim to capture the cross-character co-relationship in Chinese language, which is essential for a variety of NLP tasks. response: Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) systems have become a vital tool for computer-assisted language learning and language teaching, aiming to improve the proficiency of non-native language learners by identifying and correcting both global and local errors in their writing. The development of robust and accurate GEC systems has long been the focus of Natural Language Processing (NLP) research. In recent years, the advances of deep learning techniques, particularly Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and their variants (Sutskever et al., 2014;Cho et al., 2014;Vaswani et al., 2017), have led to many significant breakthroughs in the field of GEC (Dong et al., 2015, 2016, 2018;Gao et al., 2019). Many approaches to GEC involve treating it as a sequence-to-sequence translation task, where the model generates corrected text based on the input of the sentence with errors (Sutskever et al., 2014;Cho et al., 2014). However, traditional sequence-to-sequence models often fail to perform well in GEC tasks, especially when dealing with various kinds of errors such as word order, punctuation, or even spelling mistakes. Furthermore, traditional GEC systems rarely consider the word level structure of sentences when identifying and correcting errors. Without taking into account this local information, the model may struggle to make accurate corrections and sometimes even make new errors. Recently, a number of studies have attempted to incorporate word-level information into the GEC model, but often in a simple way, without considering the full complexity of the word level structure. In a GEC context, incorporating character-level information can also help to effectively capture the information of word and symbol-level local errors (Gao et al., 2019). However, current neural models for GEC still suffer from two main limitations. First, they rarely explore the local spatial structures of sentences from both word and character angles. Second, they fail to effectively select the optimal correction based on the relevant information in the input sequence. To fill these research gaps, this paper presents a new hybrid neural model, called Nested Attention Neural Hybrid Model (NANHM), to handle global and local errors of different types by incorporating both word and character level information. NANHM adopts a multi-stage attention mechanism for capturing word level structure information and character level information, which helps the model effectively make global and local correction based on diverse input information (Bahdanau et al., 2015;Luong et al., 2015). In contrast to previous studies, our proposed model not only considers the word-level structure but also carefully explores character level structure of input sentences, especially helpful for corrections that requires small edits in spelling or inflection. We evaluate the performance of NANHM on the CoNLL-2014 GEC development dataset (Berninger et al., 2014), which serves as the standard benchmark for GEC models (Dong et al., 2015,2016). Our experiment results show that by incorporating word and character level information, NANHM outperforms many recent state-of-the-art GEC models by significant margins. response: Quantifier Scope Disambiguation: A Fundamental Challenge In natural language processing, quantifier scope disambiguation has been an enduring challenge in linguistics and computer science. The identification of the scope of quantifiers, such as every, some, and most, in sentences is a crucial task in order to determine the intended meaning. Quantifier scope disambiguation is not a trivial task due to the inherent ambiguity of natural language. The ambiguity arises from the potential multiple ways to interpret sentences with quantifiers, making it difficult to model and algorithmically process. Sentences can have multiple valid readings and the choice between them depends on world knowledge, pragmatic information, and the context of the conversation. Current approaches to quantifier scope disambiguation have generally relied on syntactic parses and statistically grounded models, which fail to capture the complex meanings that come from pragmatic and world knowledge. For instance, if a sentence is "Some of the students studied for the exam," the sentence does not specify whether "some" refers to all the students in the group or only a subset. Understanding the correct scope of quantifiers, such as identifying whether the scope is individual-level or kind-level, is relevant for various tasks, especially for question answering, summarization, and even text-to-text tasks. A key aspect of resolving this ambiguity is considering the world knowledge as understood by humans. Pragmatic knowledge has been long recognized as a critical component of human language understanding, and its utility has been demonstrated in various applications, including argumentation mining (Lawrence and Sergienko, 2018), coreference resolution, and inference in natural language generation. Pragmatic knowledge is needed to capture the nuances of language processing, particularly when resolving ambiguous quantifier scope. However, the integration of practical knowledge into computational models has been limited due to the difficulties in representing, acquiring, and processing this kind of knowledge. In the available research on quantifier scope resolution, explicit and implicit reasoning is typically modeled via latent variables and soft constraints (Müller et al., 2016), which can be trained with annotated data. In this paper, we propose to address the ambigoyal issue using open information extraction (OIE) for extracting pragmatic knowledge from text. By leveraging OIE, we aim to extract qualitative norms that aid in determining quantifier scopes from data. Our system examines how extracted pragmatic knowledge from a corpus of subjectivity can inform the distribution of possible scope choices of quantifiers. Moreover, based on our proposed model, we can also study the desired scope permutations of quantifiers, as per general implications that guide quantifier scope. The rest of this paper will describe our OIE approach, present our proposed quantitative pragmatic knowledge, describe its formal representation in a Markov Logic Network, the relation to our quantifier scope disambiguation model and our quantitative experimental outcomes. Traditional word identification methods, where words are pre-defined based on some lexical databases, cannot effectively handle out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words or those with special characters in group conversations. Microblog texts are an even more challenging case, with the need to tackle abbreviations (e.g., "btw" for "by the way"), acronyms, numbers, and even hashtags. The demand for word segmentation processes in informal texts, including chat logs data, raises the need for the development of robust word segmentation systems to deal with varying linguistic features and write styles. Word segmentation can generally be treated as a language modeling problem where the goal is to predict the probability of a word given a set of marks, the beginning or end of a word, and the word type or part of speech (POS). In contrast to traditional word-based language models which directly predict the probability of a word given the context, word segmentation approaches are often framed as a sequence tagging problem where each word is assigned the labels that indicate its linguistic characteristics relevant for the task, especially segment, POS, and whether normalization or not should be considered. Among these devices, repetition of certain words or phrases is a common way to signal cohesion, as it creates a sense of continuity and unity between different parts of the text. The use of referring expressions is a ubiquitous feature of language, allowing writers and speakers to avoid repetition and create more concise texts by reusing the same information through different expressions. When a referring expression is used, it always refers to an antecedent, which is the expression or phrase that it denotes or recalls. The relationship between the referring expression and its antecedent is one of semantic dependency, as the referring expression relies on the meaning of the antecedent to convey its own meaning. Two types of referring expressions exist: short and long. Short referring expressions, such as pronouns, are more concise, and their meaning is closely tied to their antecedent. response: Medical named entity recognition (NER) is a crucial problem for medical text mining, which plays a key role in clinical decision support systems (CDSS), disease surveillance, and personalized medicine etc. However, developing a robust and high-precision medical NER system faces great challenges due to the following reasons. Firstly, electronic medical records (EMRs) contain diverse clinical terminologies, and writing styles of clinicians from different specialties vary significantly. For example, nephrologists tend to focus on renal diseases, while cardiologists focus on cardiovascular diseases, leading to distinct notations and concepts across specialties. Secondly, medical NER datasets are particularly data-hungry, partly because there is a limit to the number of annotations that trained clinicians can provide. Large-scale datasets and corresponding annotations are required for robust and generalizable models, which involves significant human annotation efforts and costs. In fact, developing a medical NER system tailored for one specialty and then transferring it to another one is an ideal solution to the problem of cross-specialty NER However, transfer learning in this context encounters two key challenges. Firstly, the feature representations learned from one dataset can not be directly applied to other medical datasets, as the underlying relevant features and their distributions differ significantly due to the distinct specialties. This results in suboptimal transfer ability and certain domain adaptation issues. Secondly, fine-tuning can exacerbate the issue of overfitting if not performed with great care because medical datasets from different specialties, although differing significantly, do relate closely to the medical entity of interest. Therefore, overfitting may extremely degrade the generalization ability of the transferred model across specializations. In this paper, we propose a label-aware double transfer learning framework (La-DTL) to overcome the above challenges and effectively adapt a medical NER system designed for one specialty to others with minimal annotation efforts. We harness two types of transferability: (i) the first involves using label-aware maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to learn an informative and relatively constant feature representation for facilitating the domain adaptation process; (ii) the second implies the double transfer learning framework (DTL) for parameter adaptability, where the transferred parameters have an upper bound that is adaptive to the target domain with label-awareness. As the framework is pervasive and can be applied to a variety of NER tasks with a transfer learning mindset, the theoretical bounds we propose in La-DTL can be extended seamlessly to enable a wide range of NER tasks across different domains. Moreover, based on diverse datasets and intrinsic domain knowledge through in-depth experiments, we will systematically evaluate the transfer learning generalization performance of La-DTL. The goal of event extraction is to identify and categorize the events mentioned in text, as well as the participants, locations, and other relevant details. In recent years, event extraction has attracted significant attention due to its potential applications in fields such as social media mining, business intelligence, and public health monitoring. Existing event extractors for social media aim to automatically identify and categorize the events mentioned in microblog posts, short messages, and other forms of informal communication. However, they suffer from two major problems. The lack of context in social media messages makes it challenging for event extractors to identify the correct temporal, spatial, and causal relationships between events. Moreover, the informal nature of social media language leads to ambiguity and vagueness, making it difficult for event extractors to accurately identify and categorize events. To address these challenges, several previous studies have proposed various techniques to enhance event extraction performance on social media. For example, one approach is to incorporate external knowledge bases such as Freebase or Wikipedia to provide more structured information about entities and events. Another approach is to utilize network analysis techniques to identify clusters of related events based on their temporal and spatial proximity. However, these approaches often require significant additional annotations or domain-specific knowledge, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called cross-genre event extraction with knowledge enrichment (CEKE). Instead of relying solely on the text of each social media message, CEKE incorporates cross-genre knowledge from a variety of external sources, including news articles, Wikipedia, and government reports. This knowledge is used to enhance the performance of event extraction by providing more structured information about entities and events, as well as by filling in gaps in the text. Our approach consists of two main components: a knowledge extraction module and an event extraction module. The knowledge extraction module is responsible for extracting structured information from a variety of external sources, including news articles, Wikipedia, and government reports. Our approach also shows better performance in terms of precision and recall, demonstrating its ability to accurately identify and categorize events while minimizing false positives and false negatives. response: Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), which is crucial for various downstream applications such as information extraction, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. In recent years, there has been a growing trend of using mixed texts, including both Chinese and English words, in modern articles, online conversations, and social media. However, due to the lack of specially annotated corpora, POS tagging for English words in mixed texts remains a challenging problem. A common practice is to tag all English words as "foreign words", which oversimplifies the complexity of the language and imposes limitations on the use of mixed texts in many applications. Traditional sequence labeling methods, such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) (Rabiner, 1989) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) (Lafferty et al., 2001), have been widely used for POS tagging tasks. However, these methods may fail to capture the subtle nuances of mixed texts, where English words are integrated into the Chinese text. For example, in Chinese-English mixed texts, some English words, such as names of people or places, can take on different parts of speech depending on their context. To overcome these limitations, we propose a method using dynamic features to tag POS for mixed texts. Our approach is based on the observation that English words in mixed texts often exhibit distinct linguistic patterns that can be captured by dynamic features, such as character embeddings, grammar rules, and contextual information. By incorporating these dynamic features into traditional sequence labeling methods, we demonstrate that our approach can improve the POS tagging performance for both pure Chinese texts and mixed texts. In this paper, we introduce our method for tagging POS in Chinese-English mixed texts with dynamic features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a series of benchmarks, including a newly constructed mixed text dataset. Our results show that our method achieves higher performance than traditional sequence labeling methods, and also boosts the performance of POS tagging for pure Chinese texts. The main contributions of our paper are: * We propose a novel approach for POS tagging in Chinese-English mixed texts using dynamic features. * We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on benchmark datasets. * We show that our approach can improve the performance of POS tagging for both pure Chinese texts and mixed texts. To this end, the rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the existing work on POS tagging for Chinese texts and mixed texts. In Section 3, we introduce our approach using dynamic features for POS tagging in mixed texts. In Section 4, we describe the experimental setup and results. In Section 5, we discuss the implications of our findings and potential directions for future work. In Section 6, we conclude the paper with a summary of the key contributions and insights gained. Given the increasing importance of handling mixed texts in modern NLP applications, our work on POS tagging for Chinese-English mixed texts with dynamic features is timely and relevant. We aim to contribute to the ongoing research in this area and provide insights for better handling of mixed texts in various applications.assistant This paper focuses on developing a POS tagging method specifically designed for Chinese-English mixed texts. Current entity linking systems typically rely on hand-engineered features or domain-specific training data to accomplish this task. However, these approaches have several limitations. Different senses of a word often have different distributional patterns, making it difficult for models to generalise to unseen data. response: Linguistic alignment, a phenomenon where speakers adapt their language use to match or mirror that of their interlocutors, has been extensively studied in the context of conversation and dialogue. A substantial body of research has shown that linguistic alignment is not only crucial for effective communication but also dynamically negotiates and reinforces the social relations and power structures between speakers (Bernicot et al., 2011;Dick et al., 2005;Fuselier et al., 2005). Specifically, studies have found that the relative social power between dialogue partners affects linguistic alignment, with interlocutors of higher power receiving more alignment than those of lower power (Blickle, 1979;Koenig, 1985;Kunkel and Holles, 2014). A prevalent explanation for this phenomenon is that higher-power speakers have more linguistic freedom and autonomy, which enable them to have more control over the linguistic content and structure of the conversation (Blickle, 1979). As a result, higher-power speakers tend to receive more linguistic alignment from their lower-power interlocutors, which is seen as a form of social compliance and deference. This perspective is highly influential in relevant research fields, including power dynamics, language and social psychology, and organizational communication. However, these findings and explanations have some important limitations. First, many of these studies rely on observational data and do not control for potential confounding variables that may influence linguistic alignment. Conventional feature representations in SMT are manually designed, and they rely heavily on linguistic intuition and domain-specific knowledge. However, manually designing features can be time-consuming, labor-intensive, and sometimes even less effective due to the complexity of the translation task. In recent years, deep learning techniques have made significant contributions to feature learning in SMT (Mikolov et al., 2010;Sutskever et al., 2011;Zaremba et al., 2014). Auto-encoders (AEs), a type of unsupervised neural network, have been widely used to learn feature representations from raw data (Vincent et al., 2010;Ranzato et al., 2007). The conventional method of training AEs is typically unsupervised, where the model is often over-optimized to reconstruct the input features, leading to biased and irregular feature distributions. Moreover, traditional deep auto-encoder (DAE) models usually map the input space to a lower-dimensional latent space, which can limit their ability to generalize and capture relevant features for SMT tasks. In this paper, we propose learning semi-supervised deep auto-encoder (SPT-DAE) features for phrase-based translation models, combining the benefits of unsupervised pre-training with the guidance of weakly labeled data. By pre-training with the deep belief net (DBN) on unlabeled data, we initialize the DAE parameters to capture relatively stable features. Meanwhile, we use the original input features as a teacher signal for semi-supervised fine-tuning, adapting the DAE updates to preserve the desired features while correcting the misaligned and distorted ones. With the rising popularity of conversational interfaces, there is an increasing need for developing effective and efficient methods to generate human-like responses automatically. Traditional machine translation models and neural networks have been widely applied to this task, but the generated responses often suffer from non-informativeness, such as providing generic or redundant answers (Zhang et al., 2015) or generating lengthy or combinatorial responses (Li et al., 2016). The demand for more intelligent and informative response generation methods has therefore been growing rapidly. The key to the proposed method is to effectively avoid producing responses of low quality (i.e., "safe responses") while generating high-quality responses that closely match human-written ones. In this sense, this work is motivated by the concept of" safe conversation" (Li et al., 2016). A safe conversation should be one in which the response is informative and coherent, rather than perfunctory. To overcome existing issues with non-informative response generation in neural response generation models, we propose a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) setup for modeling single-turn short-text conversations. In the Generative Adversarial approach, the ability to generate human-like responses is matched with a differentiable measure for quality, i.e., the difference between humanwritten responses and computer-generated ones. In the training, our generator takes the input and its response as a pair of inputs and generates a response based solely on the input. However, identifying and recommending relevant anecdotes is a challenging task, as it requires a deep understanding of the discourse structure and meaning of the anecdote. In the present work, we introduce a novel task called Anecdote Recognition and Recommendation. This task addresses the problem of automatically identifying and recommending relevant anecdotes that can be used as evidence to support argumentative writing or as a clue for further reading. At the heart of the Anecdote Recognition task lies a novel representation of an anecdote as a structured tuple <person, story, implication>. Here, the person refers to the protagonist of the anecdote, the story is a narrative description of events in which the person is involved, and the implication captures the meaning and topic of the anecdote. This representation is inspired by the Fragment and Event Model (FEM), which is a popular framework for modeling narrative discourse (Ashwell and Quadrado, 2006). To achieve this, we begin by applying DRI to identify the discourse roles of a text, such as thesis, main idea, and support. These roles help to locate the stories and their implications in the essay. We then use ER to identify specific entities mentioned in the story, including people and organizations, and link them to the discourse roles. This enables us to recognize the person and the story in the anecdote. They represent words as dense vectors in a high-dimensional space such that semantically similar words are mapped to nearby points. A significant problem arises, however, when words are polysemous, or have multiple senses. For example, the English word "bank" can refer to a financial institution or the side of a river. Current Word Embeddings models either ignore the polysemy of words, losing valuable meaning, or learn distinct but non-overlapping representations for each sense of a word, at the expense of requiring annotated training data for the specific sense distinctions of interest. Both approaches suffer from one or more of the following: the word's sense is inherently ambiguous and not well-captured, an explicit sense annotation task with predefined sense codes is required during training, or the learned embeddings are too sparse and not as effective for various NLP applications as monosemous embeddings. To address these deficiencies, we introduce disambiguated skip-gram, a novel, neural-probabilistic model, to learn multi-sense distributed representations of words. Disambiguated skip-gram, as the name suggests, is based on the popular skip-gram algorithm to predict the context of a word. Unlike previous probabilistic models for learning multi-sense embeddings, disambiguated skip-gram is end-to-end differentiable, which makes it possible to train using standard backpropagation and interpret as a simple feed-forward neural network. This ensures the flexibility and interpretability of the model and the mitigates the requirement for expensive human annotation. response: Conversational systems have been widely used in various applications such as customer service, search engines, and chatbots. These systems are generally designed to respond to a specific set of input queries or user requests, known as a dialogue act, such as booking a flight or searching for a specific topic. However, most conversational systems are designed with a predefined set of response strategies, and their responses are typically limited to the scope of their pre-defined dialogue acts. This type of conversational system is often referred to as a "closed-domain" conversational system. The success of conversational systems has led to an increasing demand for conversational interfaces that can handle open-domain conversations (Galley et al., 2019), where the user and the conversational system can engage in natural conversation about a wide range of topics, without an explicit dialogue act. Developing an effective open-domain conversational system requires not only the ability to generate coherent and natural responses but also to handle unexpected input from users, such as ambiguous or contradictory questions, which require complex reasoning to resolve. To overcome these challenges, a conversational system must possess at least two key capabilities: (1) a strong understanding of natural language, which enables it to interpret the user's input correctly, and (2) a rich set of content to draw upon, which enables it to respond naturally and relevantly to user queries. While recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) have provided robust methods for understanding natural language, generating coherent and natural responses to user queries remains a challenging problem (Sankar et al., 2019). Rule-based systems, which are based on hand-crafted rules and templates, have been widely used to achieve high-quality responses (Walker et al., 2003), but these systems require significant human effort to develop and maintain, which can be expensive and time-consuming. As an alternative to rule-based systems, retrieval-based systems have been proposed, which use a database of pre-defined response templates to generate responses to user queries (Lapata, 2015). However, these systems suffer from the same limitations as rule-based systems, including the need for significant human effort to develop and maintain the database of response templates, which can be large and complex. In this paper, we propose an architecture for an open-domain conversational system that uses natural language processing (NLP) techniques to generate high-quality responses to user queries. Our system, which we refer to as NLP-Converse, is designed to overcome the limitations of rule-based and retrieval-based systems by leveraging the strengths of NLP techniques, including natural language understanding, text generation, and dialogue management. We evaluate our system using human subjects and show that it achieves significantly better naturalness than a retrieval-based baseline and that its naturalness is close to that of a rule-based system using 149K hand-crafted rules. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: we start by describing the NLP-Converse architecture in Section 2, followed by a detailed description of our evaluation in Section 3, where we compare our system with a retrieval-based baseline and a rule-based system. Despite its importance, coreference resolution remains a challenging task, particularly when dealing with large-scale data. A key approach to coreference resolution has been based on the use of pairwise models, which evaluate the compatibility between mention pairs and aim to determine whether they refer to the same entity (Arantxa et al., 2009;Clark and Gupta, 2013). However, pairwise models suffer from several drawbacks, including difficulties in scaling to large numbers of mentions and limited representational power. They are often based on the use of simple features such as bag-of-words, word overlaps, or parse trees, and may fail to capture complex relationships and nuances in the coreference problem. For example, with the growing size of digital libraries, the advent of social media, and the need for more effective summarization of long documents, the demand for highly scalable coreference resolution methods grows increasingly important. Large-scale coreference resolution is in short a computationally intensive and very time consuming, pairwise models require features that perform a sorting operation that grows with the square of the number of mentions and heavy operations such as summing over all possible pairs of mentions. These factors severely limit the scalability and representational power of pairwise models when applied to real-world datasets of massive size. In this context, the search for more powerful and scalable coreference models is becoming increasingly urgent. Recently, a number of alternative models to pairwise coreference models have been proposed. Some of these models rely on the use of Neural Networks architectures that can significantly improve the performance of coreference resolution (Gupta et al., 2014;Jamiwal et al., 2017). Nevertheless, these models may be less scalable than pairwise models and often rely on random initialization and the use of the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm that may not converge consistently. Other alternative models to pairwise coreference models use a concept called constituent to model the semantic dependencies between the entities. In this paper we propose a novel discriminative hierarchical model for coreference resolution that leverages the use of latent sub-entities to succinctly summarize mentions. response: Dialogue systems have been increasingly recognized as a key area of research in natural language processing. Advanced dialogue management is critical to achieve more effective and efficient human-computer interactions. Recently, deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising approach for learning optimal dialogue policies. One of the most successful approaches is to employ Deep Dyna-Q (DDQ) (Wang et al., 2003), a paradigm that attempts to combine the strengths of Deep Q-Networks (DQN) (Mnih et al., 2013) and Dyna-Q (Sutton, 1990). In DDQ, an auxiliary planning phase is added to simulate interactions, which aims at improving the learning efficiency by collecting more virtual experience beyond real user interactions. However, the DDQ framework has room for improvement in terms of the quality of simulated experience, which plays a crucial role in learning high-quality dialogue policies. In many cases, the simulated experiences can be often incompatible with real-world interactions, for example, violating conversation initiation protocols or producing incompatible responses. This discrepancy in hypothetical and real interactions in DDQ's planning phase often impedes the effectiveness of the learned dialogue policy. In other words, when training DDQ with imperfect simulated experiences, it might lead to inferior performance when applying the learned policy in a real-world setting. This problem can become more pronounced in situations where conversations become increasingly complex, and high-quality simulated experiences are harder to generate. To address these limitations, we propose a Discriminative Deep Dyna-Q (D3Q) approach that incorporates an RNN-based discriminator into the original DDQ framework. The discriminator, which was originally used in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) (Goodfellow et al., 2014), is employed here to differentiate simulated experience from real user experience. This discrimination ability enables us to control the quality of simulated experience fed into the planning phase of DDQ. With D3Q, we can determine which simulated experiences should be accumulated into the experience histogram and used for learning the dialogue policy. In the other words, only the simulated data which has high similarity to real interactions would be considered as valuable training data. This control enables us to make the policy learned by D3Q more grounded in real-world human behavior and more robust to changing interactions. Traditional approaches to semantic class tagging rely on large annotated corpora and expensive supervised learning algorithms, requiring a significant amount of resources (human annotations and training data). This paper addresses the challenge of inducing domain-specific semantic class taggers in domains where such annotations are scarce or non-existent. Our research is motivated by the following question: can we develop a method to induce high-quality semantic class taggers using only unannotated domain-specific text data and a small set of seed words, without relying on external datasets or expensive supervised learning algorithms? The positive instances for one class are used as negative instances for the others in an iterative cycle.
