Despite significant advances in recent years, parsing is still a challenging problem, especially for certain types of languages or syntactic structures. A key factor underlying the difficulty of parsing is the complexity of the group of parser dependencies, which can be characterized by the inherent structure of the input text and the quality of the underlying model. Unfortunately, this complexity is not adequately captured by traditional evaluation metrics, such as perplexity or attachment score, which can provide a misleading view of parser performance. For instance, a high-accuracy parser can still have difficulty with certain dependencies, such as self-modifying dependencies or dependencies whose arguments have a depth greater than two. When combined with the nuances of language-specific syntax, this can lead to a picture of parser performance that is difficult to interpret. In this paper, we introduce the concept of dependency complexity, a new framework for evaluating the difficulty of dependency parsing. We propose several metrics that can be used to quantify this complexity, focusing on properties such as tree complexity, argument structure, and branching factor. By analyzing the distribution of relevant dependencies in a parsing benchmark, we can determine how much information about parser accuracy is available in these metrics and which of these metrics represent the most valuable additions to existing evaluation tools. We demonstrate the utility of this framework in characterizing the performance of two prominent parsing algorithms, and show how the new metrics can be used to compare the results of these parsers in a way that is both quantitative and interpretable. We also extend our framework to the task of cross-lingual parsing, where the complexity of the input text is mixed with the inherent differences in the underlying linguistic structures of the languages in question. Our analysis highlights the importance of moving beyond purely syntactic evaluation measures and towards a more nuanced understanding of the factors that govern dependency parsing performance. Most known stochastic sentence generators use syntactically annotated corpora and perform the projection to the surface in one stage. A prominent approach to obtain such vector representations is based on the use of distributions of word contexts. For instance, in Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), word contexts are represented using element-wise max or average pooling of contexts. One type of relationship that is frequently encountered in these tasks is taxonomic, which describes the hierarchical structure of a group of concepts where one concept is an ancestor of another. Examples of taxonomic relations include (1) ancestor relations like "child" and "parent" (e.g., Toyota and car), or (2) sibling relations like "Toyota" and "Honda." (2) Noise: lexical resources contain a considerable amount of noise due to inconsistencies and disparities between them, such as rival and differing classifications for the same concept. (3) Inflexibility: traditional knowledge sources are often extremely rigid in how data is organized and linked, such that even terms that are almost identical to those recorded in lexical resources often lack entries, leading to a deficiency of generalization capabilities. Given an image, image captioning involves generating a written description of its content, bridging the gap between visual and linguistic representations. Traditionally, image captioning can be divided into two sub-tasks: visual feature extraction and language generation. With the widespread use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), visual feature extraction has become a relatively solved problem. Recent studies have focused on designing more sophisticated language models and incorporating contextual information to improve the generation process. The encode-decoder (encoder-decoder) framework, where a pre-trained CNN-based feature extractor is paired with an attention-based decoder, has become the de facto architecture for image captioning (Xu et al., 2015;Vinyals et al., 2015). This framework enjoys the advantages of both convolutional and recurrent grids and is able to selectively focus on image regions that are relevant to the caption (i.e., attention). However, it has been found that mainstream caption generation approaches perform better in some specific aspects such as giving relevant descriptions for the image or generating complete and connected sentences. To achieve detailed captions, a type of visual attention is often considered, which allows the model to selectively focus on the most relevant image regions (Xu et al., 2015;Lu et al., 2017). response: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) is a central task in natural language processing (NLP), serving as a fundamental component for numerous downstream applications, such as question answering (QA), sentiment analysis, and text classification. Hundreds of STS systems have been proposed to determine the similarity between two texts, aiming to automate the human evaluation process. For an NLP system designer, however, selecting the most suitable STS system can be a daunting task due to the multitude of options available. A common approach to address this challenge is to conduct intrinsic evaluations, which compare the output of the STS system to human judgments on semantic similarity. The comparison is typically performed using the Pearson correlation coefficient, as it is a widely accepted measure of the linear relationship between two variables. Nevertheless, we argue that relying solely on intrinsic evaluations with Pearson correlation may be misleading. In this paper, we investigate three common STS-based tasks, where we observe that the Pearson correlation was particularly ill-suited to detect the best STS system for each task. In contrast, other evaluation measures, such as Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Divergence measures, proved to be more effective in identifying the top-performing STS system. Intrinsic evaluation is a necessary step in assessing the performance of STS systems, as it allows for objective and systematic evaluation. However, the validity of an intrinsic evaluation is not guaranteed, as it is vulnerable to the choice of evaluation metric. In this paper, we define a framework for assessing the validity of intrinsic evaluations, considering the properties of the targeted task. Specifically, we analyze the task characteristics, such as the complexity of the task, the scale of the ratings, and the noise level in the human judgments. Our framework provides insights into the limitations of the intrinsic evaluation and highlights the importance of selecting an evaluation metric that aligns with the task requirements. Furthermore, we explore alternative intrinsic evaluation methods, such as learning to rank and meta-evaluation, which have shown promising results in identifying the best STS system for a task. Our experiments demonstrate that these methods outperform Pearson correlation in selecting the top-performing STS system for each task. In addition, we investigate the impact of incorporating task-oriented knowledge into the intrinsic evaluation, which significantly improves the performance of the evaluation metrics. Our findings have significant implications for the selection of STS systems and the design of intrinsic evaluation methods. A key challenge in NLG is to develop a system that can generate varied and natural responses, not constrained by rules and heuristics. Current statistical models for NLG aim to overcome these limitations by using large amounts of training data and employing sophisticated architectures. However, the majority of these approaches fall short in terms of controllability and interpretability, making it a significant challenge to develop a system that can effectively capture the complexities of human language. The success of spoken dialogue systems is highly dependent on the quality of the generated responses. Research in NLG aims to develop robust models that can mimic human language use, incorporating contextual and pragmatic knowledge to ensure the generated responses meet certain criteria, such as fluency, coherence, and informativeness. Despite the progress made in NLG, the lack of control over generated responses is a major shortcoming that makes it difficult to scale the system to varied domains and languages. Recent approaches in NLG have relied heavily on statistical models, particularly sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models, which achieve state-of-the-art results but fail to provide an integrated and semantically controlled processing of linguistic meaning. Furthermore, current NLG systems have a tendency to produce over-specialised and non-idiolectal responses, lacking the variability and nuance of human language. In this context, the search for more flexible and interpretable models that can effectively combine high-level task completion and surface realisation remains an open challenge. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks have emerged as a suitable choice for tackling the complexities of NLG. The ability to capture a wide range of dependencies, from short-range to long-range, makes LSTMs an attractive option for modelling complex linguistic structures. However, the vanilla LSTM generator has been shown to struggle with generating coherent and varied responses due to its tendency to stick to a limited set of patterns. In an attempt to address these limitations, our proposed approach employs a semantically conditioned LSTM, thereby allowing it to learn more about sentence planning and surface realisation. Words like "good" are associated with smiling faces, and "heavy" evokes a physical image of weight. Recognizing and modeling such nuances in word meanings have occupied researchers for several years. Moreover, we use linguistic expressions to describe the world around us, and consequently words acquire meanings rooted in our perceptual experiences. While these features have exhibited good performance on lightly polysemous words, their limitations have been clearly observed, particularly on densely polysemous words. Incorporating contextual information from large unannotated corpora could potentially remedy these limitations and result in improved WSD performance. response: The structure and composition of a language are fundamental aspects of human communication. Compounding is a pervasive process in many languages, where two or more words are combined to form a new word that carries a specific meaning not found in its constituent parts. The study of German compounds is particularly interesting, as they are an essential part of the language, allowing speakers to convey complex ideas and concepts in a concise and efficient manner. Despite the importance of compounds, the mechanisms governing their meaning and potential compositionality remain poorly understood. This issue is further complicated by the vast range of semantic nuances and contexts in which compounds are used. In order to uncover the underlying semantics of German compounds, researchers have traditionally employed qualitative approaches, such as using linguistic intuition or relying on dictionaries and thesauri to categorize compounds according to their meanings. However, these methods tend to be labor-intensive and often lack the scalability necessary to analyze the many compounds that exist in the German language. A quantitative approach to understanding compound meaning is therefore highly desirable. Horn clauses are a special case of first-order clauses that do not contain positive occurrences of variables, and whose only allowed form is either the empty clause or a single positive literal. response: Named entity recognition (NER) and named entity typing (NET) are two fundamental natural language processing (NLP) tasks that have garnered significant attention in recent years. NER involves identifying named entities in unstructured text and classifying them into predefined categories, such as person, organization, or location. In contrast, NET goes a step further by group-ing named entities into subcategories, allowing for more precise understanding of the entities and their relationships. Traditional NET approaches rely on a set of predefined categories or ontologies, such as those provided by WordNet's super fine-grained type system (Miller, 1995). However, manually annotating a large dataset with such fine-grained types can be an onerous task, and existing systems often grapple with data scarcity and noise. In light of these challenges, researchers have proposed various approaches to enhance the performance of NET systems, including the use of contextual information, neural networks, and ensemble methods (Bhargava et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2017). However, these approaches often fall short in exploiting the full potential of fine-grained types, leading to a lack of granularity in extracted types. Furthermore, many existing systems heavily rely on supervision in their extractors, requiring large amounts of labeled data to train and fine-tune their models. This limitation can be crippling for NET applications in low-resource languages or domains where labeled data is scarce. To address these issues, we propose FINET, a context-aware fine-grained named entity typing system that leverages a sequence of multiple extractors and word-sense disambiguation techniques to generate candidate types. Unlike existing systems, FINET does not rely on supervision in its extractors, instead relying on WordNet and other resources to generate training data for type selection. response: Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have led to the rise of various neural network-based architectures. A remarkable group of models that continue to pique the interest of researchers are character-aware neural networks, where character-level features serve as the primary input to models for tackling various NLP tasks. Despite the prevalence of these models, an intriguing group of questions regarding their inner workings remains unanswered. When evaluating the performance of these models, one typically resorted to quantitative measures. However, it is equally essential to provide an in-depth qualitative analysis of the rules and patterns learned by these models to shed more light on their decision-making process. This raises the question of whether character-aware neural networks effectively discovering meaningful linguistic rules. The answers to these questions are far from definite, and accordingly, it is necessary to study the patterns learned by these networks more thoroughly with the aim of establishing a better understanding of how they perform at different levels of linguistic abstraction. A convincing methodology for investigating these patterns is to extend and apply the contextual decomposition, which was originally developed to demonstrate how LSTM networks for document-level sentiment classification, are actually combining more syntactic, compositional features at the document level to predict the sentiment, to relevant architectures for character-aware processing tasks, such as morphological tagging. With this study, it is possible to unlock the intrinsic rules behind the morphological tagging classification decisions made by convolutional neural networks(CNNs) and bidirectional long short-term memory (Bi-LSTM) networks. Here, we explore three datasets spanning differents languages whose solutions are deeply rooted in symbolic knowledge bases. In this study, three languages, such as Polish, Spanish and German with vastly different morphological richness but also a common platform for processing roots, prefixes, and suffixes is designed. Our hypothesis here is that models with a potential capacity for describing form and sense will stress micrograined discrete representations over a-S low-level processes - e.g., learning substrings and sequences found in the dataset. Our purpose is to trace the linguistic roots facilitating the morphological tagging to the hidden layers of the networks. One of the compelling questions is whether these networks come across actual linguistic patterns within the different linguistic environments where each word has its native sense versus use free selections. Despite recent advances in deep learning models, NER systems still rely on large amounts of manually-labeled training data, which can be time-consuming and costly to obtain (Ratinov and Roth, 2009). To address this limitation, researchers have investigated the use of distant supervision, which leverages external dictionaries to assign labels to entities in a given text (Roth and Yih, 2007). However, the generated noisy labels from distant supervision pose significant challenges to learning effective neural models (Chelikowsky et al., 2016). Distant supervision labels tend to be noisy for several reasons. Firstly, the dictionary-based approach often produces incorrect or incomplete labels due to the limitations of the dictionary (Meyer et al., 2015). Secondly, the dictionary may not cover all entities in the test data, leading to missing labels (Ono, 2011). Finally, the dictionary-based approach may assign multiple labels to the same entity, which can lead to label noise (Suchanek et al., 2007). Figure 1 illustrates the label noise problem in distant supervision. We identify two main challenges in addressing the label noise problem in distant supervision. Firstly, the traditional sequence labeling framework is not designed to handle noisy labels, which can lead to suboptimal performance (Collobert et al., 2011). Secondly, the noisy labels can propagate through the model and affect the performance of downstream tasks (Grover et al., 2013). To address these challenges, we propose a revised fuzzy CRF layer to handle tokens with multiple possible labels. response: Representing documents in a numerical form that is amenable to machine learning algorithms has been a long-standing goal of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Traditional methods, such as term frequency-inverse document frequency (tf-idf) (Jones, 1972), have been widely used. However, they fail to capture the semantic meaning of words. To address this limitation, Distributional Semantic Models (DSMs) (Baroni and Lenci, 2010) have been proposed. DSMs represent words as continuous vector space where semantically similar words are mapped to nearby points. To use these vector representations for document analysis, the Paragraph Vector (PV) (Le and Mikolov, 2014) has been proposed. PV is a type of distributional word representation that treats a paragraph as a single entity and learns an aggregate vector representation. Although PV has been widely used in various NLP tasks (e.g, Information Retrieval, Question Answering), it has several shortcomings. Firstly, it assumes that each document is a single entity, ignoring the potential multi-topic document nature. Secondly, the PV is typically dense, which can require high memory and computational resources. Thirdly, PV cannot capture complex semantic relationships, especially for short documents. To address these limitations, a number of improvements to PV have been proposed, including Softmax-based Paragraph Vector (SPV) (Gao et al., 2018), Noise Contrastive Estimation (NCE) (Mikolov et al., 2013) and Nonnegative Sparse Paragraph Vector (NSPV) (Liu et al., 2015). Considerable research efforts have focused on identifying named entities (NEs) in monolingual texts, such as person names, locations, and organizations. Yet, concurrently extracting and aligning NEs across different languages poses a multitude of challenges. Prior approaches mainly fall into two categories: rule-based methods and machine-learning-based solutions. Rule-based approaches heavily rely on domain knowledge and linguistic expertise to either postulate NE correspondences or design sophisticated mapping heuristics. However, they suffer from limited data coverage and inadequate adaptability. Most word representation learning methods rely on the distributional hypothesis, which states that words that are used in similar contexts tend to possess similar meanings. This approach has been successful in capturing the semantic nuances of words but falls short in situations where the context does not fully reveal the intended meaning, particularly in the domain of emotions. response: Sentiment analysis, a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), has been extensively applied in various domains such as product review, tweets, and social media platforms to predict the user's perception or attitude towards a product, service, or idea. With the ever-growing amount of user-generated content, the quality and reliability of sentiment analysis systems have become increasingly important. However, classic sentiment analysis techniques are limited by the ignoring of user and product contexts that significantly influence the meaning and intensity of text (Li et al., 2010;Hu et al., 2013). To address these issues, incorporating user and product information into traditional sentiment analysis models has been shown to be beneficial (Keshtkar et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2017), especially in cases where the number of reviews for users or products with limited reviews is not sufficient to train robust models, i.e. the cold-start problem in recommendation systems (Berkovsky et al., 2010). The difficulty of handling the cold-start problem mainly stems from the limited availability of user and product information which is pivotal to traditional collaborative filtering methods (Resnick et al., 1994). As relevant user and product embeddings are essential for various NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, previous research has focused on incorporating certain context-agnostic representations, such as word embeddings (W3R14) and bag of words (W3O14). However, such simple methods, although efficient, fail to capture the subtle semantic relations between users and products and are prone to over-smoothing due to the dimension reduction process (Li et al., 2016). Recently, more progressed approaches like graph-based methods (Gao et al., 2017) and multi-task learning (Zhang et al., 2020) have been proposed to represent both users and products, nevertheless, they often rely on complex compositional frameworks and numerous hyperparameters to be fine-tuned, and thus lack an intuitive understanding of latent relations and suffer from a slow training process to accommodate large-scale datasets. Moreover, most of these sophisticated approaches ignore the distributional disparities across cold-start and well-start user/product documents, causing poor performance in cold-start scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose Hybrid Contextualized Sentiment Classifier (HCSC), consisting of a fast word encoder and Cold-Start Aware Attention (CSAA) for efficient and accurate sentiment classification with a focus on handling the cold-start problem effectively. The next section describes the proposed architecture and model details in-depth through discussing the fastword encoder and the mechanism of CSAA. Subsequently, experiments and analysis are presented to exhibit the superiority of HCSC in conjunction with its computation efficiency over existing methods in sentiment analysis tasks. The paper concludes with a summary of our main contributions and how our future work can possibly mitigate related limitations. It also follows a dynamic pooling strategy accompanied by a Trackable LSTM to enlarge the receptive field and achieve output feature vectors. response: The representation of word meaning has been a long-standing problem in the field of linguistics and artificial intelligence. Traditional approaches to studying semantic representation rely heavily on linguistic information, such as co-occurrence patterns and lexical definitions, assuming that word meaning can be learned solely from the linguistic environment. However, a growing body of evidence from various disciplines, including psychology, neuroscience, and philosophy, suggests that language is grounded in perception and action (Barsalou, 2008;Gentner, 1982). This idea has led to a reconceptualization of semantic representation, emphasizing the role of sensorimotor experience in shaping word meaning. The notion of grounded cognition posits that abstract concepts, including those represented by words, are derived from concrete perceptions and bodily experiences (Wilson, 2002). In this context, researchers have started to explore the integration of linguistic and perceptual data to create more comprehensive models of semantic representation. One promising approach is to use naturally occurring corpora to approximate linguistic information, such as co-occurrence patterns and lexical definitions (Turian et al., 2010). Perceptual data can be approximated using feature norms, which capture the attributes native speakers consider important in describing the meaning of a word (Kilner et al., 2012). For example, the concept of "dog" can be associated with attributes such as "furry," "four-legged," and "friendly." By leveraging both linguistic and perceptual data, researchers can create more nuanced and sophisticated models of word meaning. However, the integration of linguistic and perceptual data poses significant challenges, such as mitigating noise and idiosyncrasies in the data, and determining how to combine the two modalities in a principled manner. In this paper, we present a comparative study of several models that represent word meaning based on linguistic and perceptual data. The models differ in terms of the mechanisms by which they integrate the two modalities, ranging from simple concatenation to more complex hierarchical combinations. We evaluate the models using human data, including similarity judgments and classification tasks, to assess their ability to capture the nuances of word meaning. Our results suggest that a closer correspondence to human data can be obtained by uncovering latent information shared among the textual and perceptual modalities, rather than arriving at semantic knowledge by concatenating the two. Recent advances in machine learning and natural language processing have improved inference performance on monolingual data, but automatically extending these systems to multiple languages remains open. response: Dialogue structure analysis is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), which refers to the process of identifying and segmenting a dialogue into coherent and meaningful components, such as utterances, turns, and topics. It plays a crucial role in various applications, including dialogue summarization, intent recognition, and human-computer interaction. Traditional approaches to dialogue structure analysis often rely on manually crafted rules or lexicons, which can be time-consuming, expensive, and do not generalize well to different domains or contexts. Furthermore, these methods typically require a large amount of labeled data to train, which is not always available. Recent advancements in data-driven methods have led to the development of machine learning models that can learn to identify dialogue structures without explicit programming or hand-crafted rules. Among these models, neural network-based approaches have shown impressive performance in various NLP tasks. However, most existing neural network models for dialogue structure analysis are designed for supervised learning, which require a large amount of labeled data to train. This limitation hampers their applicability to scenarios where labeled data is scarce or impossible to obtain. Our goal in this paper is to fill this gap by developing an unsupervised learning model that can identify dialogue structures without any labeled data. To address this problem, we propose a novel unsupervised learning model, called the hidden softmax sequence model (HSSM), based on a Boltzmann machine. The HSSM is designed to capture the hierarchical and sequential nature of dialogue structures by employing multiple types of hidden units. Specifically, our model has three types of hidden units: softmax units, which represent the latent states of utterances; binary units, which represent the latent topics specified by dialogues; and a global general topic unit, which represents the shared topic across the whole dialogue corpus. Moreover, the HSSM includes extra connections between adjacent hidden softmax units to model the dependency between the latent states of adjacent utterances. Our model offers several advantages over existing approaches. Firstly, the unsupervised learning capability of HSSM eliminates the need for manually labeled data, making it suitable for scenarios where labeled data is rare or difficult to obtain. Secondly, the hierarchical structure of our model allows it to capture the nested relationship between different dialogue components, such as utterances and topics. Finally, the probabilistic nature of our model enables it to model the uncertainty and variability inherent in human dialogue. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of the HSSM on two large-scale dialogue corpora: Twitter-Posts and Air-Ticket-Booking. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms several state-of-the-art unsupervised methods in both corpora, showcasing its effectiveness and robustness in dialogue structure analysis. Traditional dependency parsing methods typically rely on manually designed features and annotated data to induce a dependency grammar from a given corpus (Collins, 1996; Cooper et al., 2003). However, annotating corpora with dependency structures is a time-consuming and expensive process. Unsupervised dependency parsing, on the other hand, aims to learn a dependency grammar from text annotated with only part-of-speech (POS) tags, which can be obtained more easily (Ney et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014). A number of features and inductive biases have been proposed to incorporate prior knowledge into unsupervised dependency parsing. For instance, the use of manually designed features capturing the correlations between POS tags (Matsubara et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017) and the incorporation of special prior distributions to encode such information (Joshi et al., 2012) have been proposed. However, these approaches often require significant feature engineering effort and may not be easily transferable to new languages or domains. Furthermore, some of these approaches may also rely on pre-defined POS tag relationships, which can be biased towards particular linguistic patterns. Recent advances in neural networks have shown promise for unsupervised dependency parsing by learning dense and distributed representations of words and POS tags (Collobert et al., 2011; Socher et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2016). The nowadays most widely used and effective method to evaluate the similarity between text documents is based on the Bag-of-Words (BoW) representation, which represents each document as a vector of word frequencies. While BoW-based methods have been successful in many applications, they neglect the crucial relationships between words, such as semantic relationships like synonyms, antonyms, and hyponyms, which can be very informative for document similarity tasks. The dominance of word co-occurrence in the BoW representation may also lead to many irrelevant or unintended words being included as features, reducing the representation's effectiveness. Moreover, BoW representations do not take into account the structure and organization of the text, an important aspect of document meanings that may provide valuable information for document similarity tasks. To address these limitations, and build upon the benefits of graph-based models in capturing semantic relationships and structural patterns, we have developed a novel graph kernel for document similarity based on the shortest-path graph kernel. Our approach treats each document as a graph-of-words, where each word is a node, and the edges between the nodes capture the various relationships between the words in the text. Specifically, to construct the graph of-words for a given document, we can extract the stopwords and common words, such as pronouns, conjunctions, etc., from the training text and define them as nodes in the graph. For instance, we can use part-of-speech (POS) tagging and named entity recognition (NER) outputs as features to identify relevant entities and concepts in the text. To capture the relationships between these entities, we use edges that represent synsets (synonym sets), hyponyms, ontological relationships, collocations, or simply word co-occurrences. With this graph-of-words representation, we can use shortest-path graph kernels to compute the similarity between two documents. The histogram kernel and R-convolution kernel are popular choices for graph kernels for document classification. The key point in these kernels is computing the number of walks (or paths) between node pairs, which can capture higher-order relationships between words in the text. However, they may lead to high computational costs. response: Generating and following natural language instructions for complex sequential tasks represents a fundamental challenge in artificial intelligence and natural language processing. A key challenge in this area is that instructions often require the listener to carry out a sequence of actions, where each action relies on the successful outcome of the previous one. Taking a simple example, consider the instruction "Lift the heavy box, then carry it to the table, and place the object on top." In this case, the listener must unpack the potential sequential actions contained in the instruction and perform them in the correct order. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of understanding language processes and incorporating pragmatic reasoning to improve the generation and interpretation of instructions (Bisk et al., 2016). Unlike most natural language tasks, which are typically scoped to isolated, individual actions or objects, complex instructions often rely on an intricate understanding of context and the interplay between multiple actions, objects, and participants. A key challenge for natural language models that generate instructions is that it is critical to anticipate how the listener will interpret and act upon the generated instructions. For a pragmatic speaker model, the objective is to reason about why speakers produce specific instructions for a given task. This involves understanding the linguistic and extralinguistic factors that influence speaker choices, such as prior knowledge of the listener's psychology, ability, and context. To represent the pragmatic speaker, we can modify the listener model to simulate the interpretation of candidate descriptions. This thought experiment is useful for developing a speaker model that takes into consideration how its intended listeners are likely to interpret the speaker's output. At the same time, developing a pragmatic listener model enables us to simulate how listeners would process the speaker's output. Our extension to tasks with sequential structure involves processing a sequence of instructions that describe the performance of a sequence of actions. Our key contribution is the extension of these models, both listener and speaker, to sequential tasks. This involved developing a set of architectural modifications to handle the sequential structure of complex tasks and designing evaluation protocols to assess the benefits of pragmatic inference. In our main evaluations, we show that pragmatic inference significantly improves listener performance (correctly interpreting human instructions) and speaker performance (correctly generating instructions interpreted by humans) in diverse settings. In order to enable the listener model to process the sequential structure of complex instructions, we used a hierarchical neural architecture that combines the strengths of sequence-to-sequence models with the ability to compose more general policies for sequential action selection. We also developed a collection of protocols to assess the benefits of pragmatic inference for diverse instruction-following tasks, through a battery of standard permutations of instructions in a range of real-world test settings. In both our main experiments, we found that the addition of explicit pragmatic reasoning significantly improved state-of-the-art listener models and speaker models on a broad spectrum of tasks, highlighting the need to take a bottom-up and holistic view of natural language processing for understanding how language generates and follows instructions. response: Online forums or bulletin board systems (BBS) have become a vital platform for people to share information, exchange ideas and ask for help (Mills and Steinfield, 2006;Herring, 2007). They serve as a bridge connecting people and bridging the gap of information between experts and non-experts. In an online group, users can share their experiences, exchange stories related to a topic and even get help from others (Koutrika et al., 2010;Sakaki et al., 2010). The online forum is generally divided into multiple hierarchical threads which consist of a series of posts discussing a specific question or topic. Thread discussions can broadly be categorized into two main types - "Q/A" and the constructive depth of discussion. A PCFG is a particular type of grammar in which each rule has an associated probability. This allows us to generate parse trees and estimate the probability of each tree. The PCFG model is widely used in NLP tasks such as parsing, machine translation, and language modeling because it allows us to capture hierarchical structure in the data. response: Disentanglement of interleaved text conversations is an essential task in various natural language processing applications, such as chatbots, conversational dialogue systems, and social media monitoring. The primary goal of this task is to automatically group overlapping sequences of messages into separate conversations, thereby enabling computational processing of text exchanged in interactive venues. Current disentanglement methods exploit both lexical and non-lexical information present in conversations for this task. Lexical features are typically represented using static word representations (e.g., word embeddings), which capture certain aspects of word meanings based on their co-occurrence patterns. While effective in many natural language processing tasks, these methods largely ignore the rich contextual information that exists in conversations. Contextual information is crucial for understanding the meaning of a message, as it captures the nuances of human communication, including anaphora (e.g., pronoun reference), deixis (e.g., actor or location orientation), and inferences that require understanding the context in which a message was generated. Context-aware approaches typically require access to structured contextual information, such as document-level or clause-level annotations, which are often difficult to obtain or may be expensive to create. Moreover, many contextual properties relevant for disentanglement might remain hidden, thus eluding human perception, even skilled annotators. For example, some contextual properties are not explicitly available but can be inferred implicitly. Since contextual properties potentially affect message disentanglement significantly, we propose a novel, computationally efficient approach that captures both explicit and implicit contextual properties of messages to disentangle interleaved conversations. Our method, dubbed Contextual Message Expansion (CME), is grounded in Probability theory and employs a probabilistic expansion mechanism to generate a richer representation of each message that considers the temporal context and social information associated with each participant in a conversation. Specifically, CME extends the given message through automatic augmentation with contextual markers (e.g., recipient labels, relative time expressions) and a set of structured constraints (message purpose, topic histogram), thereby enriching the information content of each message. To this end, we develop a novel probabilistic model that predicts the conditional probability of each augmented message. response: Chinese word segmentation (CWS) is a fundamental problem in Chinese natural language processing. It aims at segmenting Chinese text into individual words, which is a prerequisite for many natural language processing applications such as information retrieval, machine translation, and sentiment analysis. Supervised learning is currently the most effective method for CWS, and it performs well when a large-scale annotated corpus is available. However, it is challenging to use supervised learning methods when dealing with out-of-domain texts, where annotated data is scarce or even non-existent. In fact, most CWS datasets were created based on a specific domain, and they may not perform well when applied to other domains, such as technical documents, news articles, or social media posts. Current state-of-the-art CWS methods rely heavily on labeled training data and often fail to generalize well to new domains without sufficient labeled data. For instance, CWS performance significantly drops when applying a model trained on the Penn Chinese Treebank (CTB) to a out-of-domain corpus such as the technical document corpus CSTC (Xue et al., 2004). Figure 2 illustrates the performance of the popular CWS model, the Stanford segmenter (Tseng et al., 2005), on various domains. In this paper, we propose a novel corpus expansion approach to address the out-of-domain problem in CWS. Our goal is to leverage the massive redundant information on the Web to automatically expand the training corpus for out-of-domain texts. There are many issues to consider when using the Web for corpus expansion. Firstly, Web data is highly noisy and may contain errors, which can be even more detrimental when using Web data for corpus expansion. Secondly, Web data may not reflect real-world language patterns that vary across domains. However, the redundancy and diversity of Web data provide a valuable resource that can be exploited to improve CWS performance. By leveraging the low-hanging fruits of available Web information, we can create a reliable and diverse annotated dataset for CWS that complements existing labeled datasets. Building on these insights, we outline a novel approach to automatic corpus expansion for CWS, which we refer to as WebAug. This approach is designed to break the limitation of CWS models on out-of-domain texts by leveraging the redundancy and diversity of Web information. Its main goal is to estimate the probability distribution over an entire sequence of words in a sentence. Despite the significant advances in recent years, traditional language models often suffer from a major limitation: they tend to fail when confronted with out-of-domain (OOD) tasks. This is because they are designed to learn patterns and structures specific to the in-domain data, and therefore exhibit poor generalization to unseen domains. This limitation is particularly problematic in many real-world applications, where the available data often lie in a single domain, and applications of varying complexity may require models to adapt to different domains. One approach to address this issue is to use domain-invariant language models, which are trained on a set of domains, and have the ability to generalize to unseen domains. They typically employ a hierarchical prior over the model parameters, allowing for inductive transfer across related tasks and domains. response: Relation classification is a challenging task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, question answering, and text summarization. The task involves identifying the semantic relation between two entities mentioned in a text, such as ".profession" or "production location". Over the past decade, there has been a significant improvement in the experimental performance of relation classification using deep neural network architectures [Socher et al., 2013;Zeng et al., 2015;Bauer et al., 2019]. However, despite these advances, individual models have been generally evaluated on a very narrow range of datasets. For instance, the state-of-the-art (SOTA) models on the TACRED dataset [Zhang et al., 2017] are often found to be less effective on other datasets, such as CKE with Extended Dictionary [Kim et al., 2019]. This raises questions about the adaptability of the architectures across different datasets, making comparisons between approaches difficult. Moreover, the performance of relation classification models highly depends on the type of relation and the characteristics of the datasets. For example, the model performance is often better on binary relation classification [Zeng et al., 2015] compared to multi-class classification [Bauer et al., 2019]. Furthermore, some models are more suitable for different datasets with varying characteristics, such as syntax, semantics, and compositionality [Socher et al., 2013;Zhang et al., 2017]. To address these issues, there is a pressing need for a systematic and comprehensive analysis of neural relation classification architectures across multiple datasets. This paper aims to fill this gap by exploring different neural relation classification architectures across six widely used benchmark datasets: TACRED [Zhang et al., 2017], CKE with Extended Dictionary [Kim et al., 2019], Attention-SUM [Bauer et al., 2019], ERNIE-CCKE [Dong et al., 2020], MCAN [Ji et al., 2019] and runs with extended causal dictionary CMN on DSM [Kim et al., 2019]. We also propose a novel multi-channel LSTM model combined with a CNN architecture to take advantage of all currently popular linguistic and architectural features. Our 'Man for All Seasons' approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on two datasets, showing the effectiveness and flexibility of the proposed architecture across different datasets. While we achieve SOTA based on diverse datasets, in this work, we draw upon direct insights into the continued challenges faced by neural language models on relation classification. response: Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and knowledge extraction have enabled the development of knowledge-based question answering (KBQA) systems that can comprehend and answer complex questions by extracting information from large-scale knowledge graphs. KBQA systems rely heavily on efficient reasoning and query formulation methods that can transform unstructured natural language questions into structured queries that can be resolved against the knowledge graph. However, existing benchmark datasets WebQuestions and SimpleQuestions lack the capability of evaluating KBQA systems on a set of complicated questions, often referred to as multi-constraint questions. Multi-constraint questions require knowledge base relations to be combined in a specific manner to obtain the answer. The lack of suitable benchmark datasets makes it challenging to evaluate the capabilities of KBQA systems on such complex scenarios. The prominence of such scenarios may be attributed to the following facts: Firstly, users may express their queries by combining multiple clauses by 'and', 'or', or 'not' which in turn requires resolving multiple knowledge base relations for getting the final answer. Secondly, the answers to complex questions often depend on several attributes or properties from a single entity, which is more representative of the mainstream web queries. Consequently, the current state of art KBQA methods have been tuned heavily on the two benchmark datasets, resulting in poor performance when faced with these complex scenarios. This paper aims to address the above limitations in current KBQA systems by proposing a novel systematic KBQA framework that can handle multi-constraint questions by developing a fully declarative approach to resolving complex queries. Our approach is based on constraint satisfaction, where the KBQA system models the question and its constraints using constraints, such as 'forall', 'exists' and equality. Our framework includes two modules: the first is a constraint modeling module that models the constraints expressed by the question into a set of logical constraints, which may involve numerical, string, and categorical equality testing. The second is the answer resolution module that takes the set of logical constraints and a knowledge graph and returns a set of entities that satisfy the constraints. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we release ComplexQuestions, a new benchmark dataset consisting of 5,754 questions that are significantly more challenging than existing benchmark datasets. ComplexQuestions includes questions that can be solved by combining two or more relations to get the answer. In fact, compared to other natural language processing (NLP) tasks, the evaluation of GED is more complex and requires careful consideration of several issues. One of the main reasons for this complexity is the three-way contingency between a writer's sentence, the annotator's correction, and the system's output. This contingency means that a system's performance can be evaluated based on four possible outcomes: true positives (correct detection of error), false positives (incorrectly identifying non-error as an error), true negatives (correct identification of non-error), and false negatives (failing to identify an error as an error). Furthermore, another key issue that affects the evaluation of GED is the skew of the data. Since errors are relatively rare compared to non-errors, traditional measures of performance such as accuracy and precision are not necessarily accurate or meaningful. For instance, in a corpus where 99% of the sentences are error-free, a system that only correctly identifies 50% of the errors would still achieve high accuracy but is clearly not effective. While supervised morphological analysis has made significant progress in recent years, unsupervised methods remain largely underdeveloped and still suffer from a lack of generalizability and robustness across different languages (Kittel et al., 2013). In particular, the requirement of parallel data, or data from multiple languages aligned with each other, is a major obstacle to the development of data-efficient unsupervised methods. Most state-of-the-art unsupervised morphological analysis methods rely heavily on inductive bias and incorporate domain knowledge into their models (Chemla and Schapire, 2009;Harmeling, 2012). For instance, the minimum description length (MDL)-based approach of (Stolcke, 1998) employs a morphologically informed prior over possible analyses. While these approaches have shown promising results, they often rely on specific assumptions about the morphology of the target language and can fail when deployed in new languages with unanticipated characteristics. In this paper, we take a different approach to unsupervised morphological analysis and propose a novel framework based on structured nearest neighbor prediction. We treat languages with labeled data as training examples for unlabeled languages and seek to find the morphological analysis for each unlabeled language by identifying the most similar training language in a universal morphological feature space. This allows us to benefit from the knowledge encoded in the labeled training languages without assuming any parallel data. Our framework is thus a kind of multilingual learning, where languages that share the same linguistic family are used to help each other with morphological analysis. response: Domain adaptation is a challenging problem in named entity recognition (NER), which involves adapting an NER model trained on a source domain to a target domain with a different data distribution. Due to the acquisition cost and the diversity of NER annotation schemes across domains, it is difficult to obtain sufficient labeled target domain data for tuning the original model. As a result, the NER model severely degrades its performance in the target domain. This performance degradation is mainly caused by the differences in term representations between the source and target domains. For example, a personal name like "Obama" is generally related to the concept of "politics" and "president" when applied to the politics domain, whereas it is associated with "Anniversary" and "sports" when the context domain is sports. The lack of adaptations of term representations reduces the performance of existing NER models in the target domains, since the trained model may fail to generalize and recognize entities in the target domain. Domain adaptation for NER can be treated as a task of reducing the skewness in term distributions between the source and target domains, without the explicit need of labeled target domain data for the fine-tuning process. Domain adaptation approaches typically conduct label transfer, feature transformation or instance weighting. Label transfer based approaches transfer the labels from the source domain to the target domain, which often relies on plenty of labeled target-domain data. Feature transformation based approaches change the representation of features for better dealing with target domain data, such as employing the projection from the source domain features to the target domain features through multilinear mapping (Ganin and Lempitsky, 2015) or using shared-latent representations (Chu et al., 2016). Instance-weighting based methods re-weight the training instances from the source domain so that the unseen data in the target domain is either down-weighted or up-weighted (Long et al., 2015). However, learning instance-wise weights still requires some labeled target domain data. This process is relatively effortless for humans, as it relies on their commonsense knowledge and everyday experiences. For instance, the word "petal" is associated with sight, as we perceive the physical appearance of flowers, while the word " music" is related to hearing, as we experience the auditory perception of sounds. However, building a comprehensive lexicon that maps words to their respective senses is a challenging task for computational models, as it requires a robust understanding of the intricate relationships between language, perception, and cognition. Existing NLP resources, such as-word embeddings and lexical databases, provide valuable insights into word meanings but often fail to capture the multi-sensory aspects of language. A sensorial lexicon, which systematically associates words with their corresponding senses, is thus a crucial resource for various NLP applications, including sentiment analysis, text classification, and machine translation, where the context and nuances of sensory experiences can significantly impact the interpretation and generation of language. In this paper, we propose the development of a comprehensive sensorial lexicon, Sensicon, which maps English words to their respective senses. To create Sensicon, we leveraged a computational method that combines bootstrapping and corpus statistics. Our approach starts by compiling a training dataset of word-sense pairs from a subset of a large English corpus. We then utilize a machine learning algorithm to classify new word-sense pairs, progressively enlarging the training dataset through a series of iterations. The richness of the lexicon is evaluated using a gold standard dataset that was created via crowdsourcing, and we demonstrate that a simple classifier relying on Sensicon outperforms two benchmark baselines on a sensory classification task at both word and sentence levels. In order to effectively exploit information buried in large volumes of online reviews, opinion mining has emerged as a novel field of study, combining techniques from natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (Liu et al., 2005;Hatzivassiloglou et al., 2005). Sentiment analysis typically focuses on calculating a sentiment score, which is used to estimate the polarity of a text or document. The process of sentiment analysis can be performed at different levels, including document level, sentence level, and even sub-sentence level. Typical opinion mining applications include product review analysis, movie review analysis, and the analysis of public opinions about events and politics (Györkös et al., 2014). One of the fundamental tasks in opinion mining is extracting opinion targets, which can be the person, organization, product, or service being discussed. To extract opinion targets, researchers usually adopt two types of approaches: syntax based and alignment based methods. Syntax based methods, such as rule-based approaches and machine learning-based methods, rely on syntactic patterns to identify opinion targets (Wiebe et al., 2005;Reeves et al., 2007). These methods exploit the grammatical structure of sentences to determine what is being mentioned as an object of opinion. For example, in the sentence, "The new Windows 8 is terrible", the word "Windows 8" is the opinion target. However, syntax-based methods often suffer from parsing errors when dealing with online informal texts. As a result, the accuracy of the opinion target extraction is compromised. In addition, these methods typically require a large amount of labeled training data, which can be difficult to obtain, especially for small and medium-sized corpora. This problem is further exacerbated by the fact that parsing can be computationally expensive, and the performance of syntax-based methods can degrade significantly when handling large amounts of text data. In contrast, alignment based methods use word alignment models (WAMs) to identify opinion targets (Gurevych and Stein, 2007). WAMs are based on statistical machine translation technology, and have been widely used in machine translation and bilingual dictionary extraction. Unlike syntactic-based methods, word alignment methods do not require syntactic parsing, which makes them more suitable for handling informal language data. Word alignment models can capture the semantic relationships between words or phrases in different languages through statistical analysis of their permutations. This approach, however, relies on the availability of large-scale bilingual corpora, which can be difficult to obtain, especially for less widely spoken languages. Furthermore, WAMs may suffer from word-order differences between languages, which can lead to inaccurate alignment results. response: The spread of misinformation and biased news has become a central concern in today's digitally interconnected world. With the rise of the internet and social media, people are exposed to a large amount of information that is harder to verify than ever before. One of the most critical issues is the detection of biased news and the ideologies that they promote. Detecting the ideology of news articles has been a critical task that has garnered much attention in recent years due to its importance in assessing the credibility and quality of news sources. Traditional methods of detecting ideology rely heavily on keyword matching and bag-of-word based models, which are often simplistic and fall short in accurately detecting the subtle nuances of biased language (Qian et al., 2016). Moreover, previous research has shown that keyword-based methods are plagued by-word lists that can be easily circumvented by biased articles (Banerjee and Mcsherry, 2013). Furthermore, most existing works on automatic political ideology detection only leverage textual cues, ignoring other forms of information that may reveal an article's ideology more effectively. In this paper, we draw inspiration from recent advances in neural inference (Raghanathan et al., 2013) to propose a novel attention based multi-view model that leverages cues from title, textual content and link structure of news articles to identify the ideology evinced by these narratives. Our model draws on advances in representation learning in natural language processing (Gottesman et al., 2012) and network science (Groh et al., 2013) to capture cues from both textual content and the network structure of news articles. The network structure of news articles provides valuable information about the relationships between news entities, including the relationships between sensationalist and conservative news sources that often harbor similar ideologies. Our model incorporates a graph-based representation learning component to extract these network structures and represent them in a vector space (Groh et al., 2013). Additionally, we use a combination of attention and network-based semantic embedding to learn latent representations of news articles' ideological content. We empirically evaluate our model against a battery of baselines and show that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 10 percentage points F1 score, demonstrating the effectiveness of leveraging multi-view information to detect news articles' ideology. Our results highlight the importance of considering both textual and network-based cues in detecting biased language, which has major implications for the development of robust tools for the detection of misinformation in the news. With the rapid growth of the web, it has become increasingly difficult to retrieve the most relevant entities that satisfy user queries quickly and efficiently. Traditional entity retrieval methods typically view entities as vectors of attributes, and construct the query by weighting the attributes according to the query words. However, this approach has its limitations as the attributes may not accurately capture the nuanced characteristics of entities, and the query words may not effectively convey the user's intent. In this paper, we propose a novel entity representation model called entity factoid hierarchy to tackle the challenges of traditional entity retrieval methods. Our approach takes a human-centered view of entity retrieval, where users generate queries through a two-step process. In the first step, users select entity facts that can distinguish target entities from others. These facts may involve personal characteristics, relationships, behaviors, or any other attributes that make entities unique. In the second step, users choose words to describe each selected fact. For example, when searching for a hypothetical "art collector in New York City named Michael Davis," a user may first select facts such as "being the current head of art department at Sotheby's, a heavy hearted philanthropist based in NYC, having a psychology degree and donating certain artwork for non-profit causes". Generally, we nowadays see applications of such natural language interfaces in both robotics (Shakle et al., 1994) and mixed reality (Kim et al., 2008). In particular, it is particularly challenging for robots to use natural language to understand human navigation commands (Goodman et al., 2005). The main challenge is not only to translate the commands from the natural language to a robot-understandable format, but also to ensure that the robot navigation is executed safely. Current data-driven methods approach this problem by considering a robot's sensor data to compose a navigational graph and then compute a path using the graph depth-first search or shortest path algorithms (G jets et al., 2011). response: Transition-based constituent parsing has been widely used in recent years to model sentence structures. The basic idea is to represent a sentence as a state transition process, where each state represents a step in constructing the parse tree. Given a sentence, the goal is to derive a sequence of actions that corresponds to a well-formed parse tree. However, traditional transition-based parsing approaches suffer from a pipeline structure, which sequentially addresses the tasks of part-of-speech (POS) tagging and constituent parsing. The intermediate POS tags are used as an input to the syntactic parser, which not only propagates POS tagging errors but also diminishes the parsing accuracy due to the coarser, bag-of-words representation of sentences. This is known as error propagation. Another drawback is that the score of action sequences competes extensively in the beam-search decoding strategy, which makes it difficult to select the most optimal action by giving rise to the over-smoothing problem. In other words, the coarser representation of sentences, associated with short-term action sequences, discourages the parser from exploring a hypothetical local optimal shift in short-term states, since the competing action sequence, which reveals the structure at the whole parsing process, is highly likely to prevail. Furthermore, the power of transition-based parsers is limited by their narrow feature set, especially in languages with certain characteristics like Chinese. For example, in sentences with multiple clauses, traditional features fail to capture the complex relationships among words and clauses. Even with the incorporation of distant features, such as those proposed by the Stack-LSTM parser [Wu et al., 2018], which provide a coarse-grained, non-local view of the sentence, transition-based parsers still rely heavily on local word information and fail to explore the modeling power that comes from incorporating more complex, non-local word and word-cluster features. However, they are often difficult to use for those without technical expertise, as they typically require a high degree of spatial literacy and familiarity with specialized query languages (e.g. SQL). In an effort to improve the accessibility and usability of GIS, several groups have proposed developing interfaces that allow users to query Geographic Information Systems using natural language (NL), as opposed to more traditional query methods such as point-and-click interfaces or text-based commands. Despite these efforts, there are still significant challenges to be addressed in the development of NL interfaces for GIS. One major challenge is building an accurate model of the mapping from natural language to geographic queries, often called "semantic mapping". Another challenge is designing an interface that allows users to express a wide range of queries, including complex or uncertain ones, in natural language. A key element of an NL interface for GIS is a "semantic parser". A semantic parser is a computational model that can analyze a natural language query and, based on domain knowledge, infer the specific query being referred to (i.e. the image or "logical form" that the query expresses). By converting a natural language query into a query that can be executed by a GIS, a semantic parser can provide users with a powerful new way to access and interact with geographic data. However, the development of accurate semantic parsers for GIS and, more generally, for NL databases is a difficult task. It requires large amounts of annotated data, models that can accurately capture the complex relationships between geographic entities, and methods that can adapt to the inherent uncertainties of natural language. response: Dialogue analysis is a prominent research area that aims to understand the structure and dynamics of natural language interactions among humans. A fundamental challenge in dialogue analysis is measuring and modeling various aspects of dialogue quality, such as cooperation, coordination, and understanding. One essential aspect of cooperative dialogue is the exchange of appropriate and relevant information, which requires adhering to conventions and group norms. Deviation from these norms, or non-cooperation, can significantly affect the quality and outcome of the dialogue. Measuring non-cooperation is essential for understanding various aspects of dialogue, such as identifying problematic communication styles, detecting deception, and evaluating the performance of dialogue systems. Previous work on non-cooperation has relied on human evaluation, relying on annotators to assess the degree of cooperation by manually scoring the dialogue based on certain criteria. However, this method is time-consuming, costly, and often subjective. Moreover, previous research has mainly focused on modeling non-cooperation in terms of specific behaviors or actions that are considered non-cooperative, such as lying or dominating the conversation. In contrast to this categorical approach, we aim to develop a more nuanced and quantitative measure of non-cooperation by focusing on the extent to which dialogue participants deviate from relevant conversational conventions, such as the obligation to respond to a question or the obligation to ask for clarification when certain. To develop such a measure, we draw on insights from dialogue theory and pragmatics, which provide a framework for understanding the normative structure of dialogue and identifying the obligations that speakers have towards each other. Specifically, we rely on the theory of dialogue games (Ludwik Fleck, 1935;Martin Emil Krogh Jensen and Grønmo:2011), which describes dialogue as a strategic interaction between players who engage in a sequence of moves to achieve a common goal. A dialogue game is formally defined as a tuple consisting of players, moves, a scoring function, and a condition of winning. Moreover, dialogue games may include conversational norms and obligated moves that describe the duties and responsibilities of each participant in the conversation. By defining dialogue games as formal models of conversation rules and cooperative obligation fulfillment, we can systematically analyze the structure of a dialogue and identify instances of non-cooperation based on participants' deviations from these rules. In our paper, we present a novel method for measuring non-cooperation based on the concept of "dialogue games," where cooperation is seen as a normative concept based on obligatory dialogue moves. By first identifying these obligatory moves (often referred to as Gricean maxims, through inducting upon permutations of data of a co-op conversation-based game), participants' deviations from obliging such moves can be thereby predicted and scored statistically, generating quantitative measures of noncooperation in a given dialogue. Rather than just providing a static assessment of noncooperation, our method allows us to generate accurate predictions of cooperation and relative cooperation levels in both participants. This enables the evaluation of dialogue quality and identifies problematic communication styles in dialogue and, more critically, makes it possible to forecast which dialogue partner was less cooperative. By providing a way to quantify noncooperation based on conversational deviations, our approach can be used to evaluate the performance of various dialogue systems, including human-like virtual assistants, tutoring agents, and sophisticated dialogue systems, and could be used to improve these systems' behavior by penalizing non-cooperative moves.assistant Our paper also highlights the potential of combining our approach with machine learning techniques to improve the accuracy of non-cooperation

response: Keyphrase generation is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), which refers to automatically identifying a set of phrases that capture the main ideas and topics of a given text, such as a document or a paper. Keyphrases help readers quickly understand the content and context of a document, making the summarization process more efficient and effective. With the rapid growth of online content, automatic keyphrase generation has become increasingly important for Information Retrieval (IR), text classification, recommender systems, and other applications that require a concise representation of text content. Although conventional approaches to keyphrase generation have shown promising results, they often neglect the correlation among keyphrases, resulting in duplication and coverage issues. For instance, some existing methods select multiple identical keyphrases or fail to cover all important topics of a document, which reduces the effectiveness of keyphrase generation. Moreover, previous approaches often ignore the context and relation between keyphrases, leading to incompatible or irrelevant keyphrases, which may confuse readers or hamper further processing of the keyphrases. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel sequence-to-sequence architecture, named CorrRNN, specifically designed for keyphrase generation with correlation constraints. Building upon the recent advances in sequence-to-sequence learning and conditional random fields, CorrRNN effectively captures correlation among multiple keyphrases and leverages the context and relation between them. There are two key aspects of CorrRNN that capture correlation among keyphrases. Firstly, we introduce a coverage vector to monitor whether the word in the source document has been summarized by previous phrases. With this coverage vector, we can emphasize the importance of novel information and minimize the repetition of information that has already been captured by previous phrases. This can lead to suboptimal corrections, where the most appropriate preposition is not selected. For instance, when a non-native speaker writes "I go store to buy milk", the correct correction "I go to the store to buy milk" requires knowledge of the appropriate preposition usage in this context. In this paper, we focus on the task of generating candidate corrections for error correction in preposition usage made by non-native English speakers. We propose a novel approach, which generates candidate corrections by determining likely preposition confusions using an annotated corpus of non-native text. response: Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) is a popular method for optimizing the performance of machine translation (MT) systems by selecting parameter values that maximize performance on a given tuning set, typically measured by an automatic evaluation metric, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). MERT has been widely adopted in MT research and development due to its simplicity and effectiveness, particularly when the system will eventually be evaluated using the same metric. However, in real-world scenarios, most MT evaluations involve a human-based component, where human assessors evaluate the quality of translations against certain quality metrics or reference translations. This introduces a challenge in performing MERT with human-based metrics, as it requires involving human evaluators at the tuning stage, which is often impractical and expensive. Furthermore, MERT relies on a large number of candidate translations to select the optimal set of parameters, leading to the proliferation of redundant or similar candidate sentences during the tuning process. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of human-in-the-loop MERT and propose a novel approach to circumvent the need for human input at the tuning stage, while still utilizing human judgments to inform the evaluation metric. Our solution involves designing a reranking metric, referred to as RYPT (Ranking Yield Percentage Threshold), which takes human judgments into account, yet only requires human input to build a database that can be reused over and over again. In essence, RYPT combines the benefits of automatic evaluation metrics with the insights of human evaluators, providing a more accurate predictor of translation quality. This paper presents the following contributions: • We introduce the reranking metric RYPT and demonstrate its ability to account for human judgments while being scalable and efficient. • We analyze the diversity of candidate translations produced during MERT and show that redundancy can be harnessed to improve tuning efficiency and reduce testing overhead. • We illustrate the superiority of RYPT over BLEU as a predictor of translation quality, taking into account the relatively high cost and variability of human evaluation. We explore the applicability of RYPT to real-world applications and envision its potential as a more robust and cost-effective alternative to BLEU-based tuning methods. By incorporating human expertise into the training loop, we aim to boost the viability and reliability of machine translation systems in practical settings. By targeting a more holistic understanding of the translation process, we can improve the overall quality of MT systems and enable them to meet the demands of various stakeholders in the translation community. This paper aims to position RYPT as a potential catalyst for the widespread adoption of human-in-the-loop MERT and accelerating the transition towards more accurate and efficient machine translation systems. Firstly, estimating the large number of translation probabilities required by these models can be computationally expensive and often results in models with sparse probability distributions. Secondly, the discrete representations of translation units, typically based on phrase pairs or n-gram phrases, can lead to over-smoothing and poor performance on low-frequency words. Finally, a major issue is the lack of sufficient training data, which typically restricts the model to consider a small amount of context. While some models attempt to enlarge the data size available for training, the MLE approach remains essentially the same. As an alternative to MLE, a number of recent studies have explored different estimation strategies and representations of the translation units. One such family of models is continuous space translation models, which estimate translation probabilities using a continuous representation of translation units in lieu of standard discrete representations. Our goal is to evaluate the effectiveness of continuous space models for machine translation, and to propose a framework in which these models can be effectively trained and used on top of a standard n-gram translation system. We believe that continuous space representations offer several advantages over conventional discrete representations. Firstly, they potentially reduce over-smoothingand facilitate the modeling of rare or out-of-vocabulary words. Secondly, they may alleviate the need for extensive data augmentation or artificial language corpora. To further boost the training efficiency and model capacity, we propose a multi-layer neural network architecture with a specially designed SOUL (Separate Output Units Layout) structure. The proposed network is designed to handle a large set of translation units by jointly computing the representations and the associated estimates. Existing approaches to temporal relation classification typically involve extensive feature engineering, which often involves manual extraction of linguistic and temporal features from the input text, followed by the application of machine learning algorithms to predict the correct temporal relation. However, these methods can be labor-intensive, and their effectiveness is often limited by the availability of large-scale annotated datasets. Moreover, the feature engineering process can be time-consuming and require significant domain expertise, making it difficult to generalize across different NLP applications.
