response: Low-resource neural machine translation (NMT) remains an open challenge in the field of natural language processing. Despite recent advancements in multilingual and unsupervised NMT, large amounts of data are required for training high-quality NMT systems. However, many languages lack sufficient parallel data, hindering the deployment of NMT systems for these languages. A promising approach to address this challenge is multi-source and multi-target NMT (Arivazhagan et al., 2019;Fan et al., 2019), which leverages pre-trained NMT systems to translate across related languages. Nevertheless, multi-source and multi-target data may not always be available. An alternative approach to handle the lack of data is self-supervised learning (Lample and Conneau, 2019;Gupta et al., 2020), which employs tasks such as back-translation, round-trip translation, or denoising autoencoders to generate synthetic parallel data for fine-tuning. Another promising direction is meta-learning for NMT (Hou et al., 2019;Aharoni and Goldberg, 2019), which aims to train the model to adapt quickly to new languages and unseen data distributions. Meta-learning algorithms, such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) (Finn et al., 2017), were originally designed for few-shot learning in computer vision. In this work, we adapt MAML to the task of low-resource NMT, leveraging its ability to learn to adapt quickly to new languages and unseen data distributions. However, this problem is fundamentally different from typical classification problems. In classification, all instances are supposed to belong to one of the predefined classes; whereas in entity linking, there may not be a corresponding entry for an entity in the KB. Moreover, the entities in the KB that do belong to the relevant classes are often heavily unequal in quality and relevance, resulting in disorder in the truth values. In typical state-of-the-art phrase-based systems, the reordering of phrases is determined by lexicalized reordering models, such as n-gram-based models or decision trees (Galley and Manning, 2008;Galley et al., 2006). However, these lexicalized reordering models have three significant drawbacks that limit their effectiveness. Firstly, they are heavily context insensitive because the reordering probabilities are computed using only the current phrase pair, without considering the context of previous phrase pairs. response: Representation learning is a critical component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, particularly text classification. Traditional text classification models largely rely on shallow feature engineering and usually ignore the semantic information embedded in the text, hinderingtheir performance on complex tasks. With the advent of deep learning, many deep neural models have been proposed to learn representations from raw text data. However, existing models suffer from several limitations. On the one hand, some models like Word2Vec (Le and Mikolov, 2014) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) mainly learn local semantic representations based on the co-occurrence of words in the document. However, these models ignore the global structure information of the document. On the other hand, many structure-based models like Recursive Neural Networks (RNNs) (Socher et al., 2011; dai et al., 2015) rely on the manually annotated or parsed input to capture the global structure information. However, these models have significant limitations: 1) they require a tremendous amount of annotated data, which is very expensive to obtain, and 2) the structured parsing results cannot capture the linguistic complexity of natural languages, such as heavy use of relative clauses and elliptical constructions. A major design goal for text representation learning models is to automatically capture both local semantic and global structure information. A typical NMT system generates a translation by sampling a sequence of words from a probability distribution over the target vocabulary, conditioned on the source sentence and the decoder's internal state. 1 The probability distributions are usually obtained using a group of parallel recurrent neural networks and an attention mechanism. However, the main challenge with these systems is that they do not output a single translation, but rather sample from the probability distribution at each time step, resulting in a family of possible translations. To alleviate this issue, the concept of beam search was introduced, which aims at keeping the K most likely candidates at each time step (K is a hyperparameter known as beam size) by selecting the best next token at each step. One of the advantages of using beam search is that it modifies the sampled output distribution at each time step and can dramatically improve the quality of the translation in comparison to the greedily selected sequence. However, beam search also introduces several issues, one of which is that the selection process at each time step reduces the search space for the next step. This issue is compounded when the relevant candidate pool size, which is driven by the sum of the inverse of the probability of each candidate at each time step, is restricted. A second issue with beam search arises when the number of candidates that has been generated at any time step is greater than the size of the beam, which forces the algorithm to first select which subset of candidates to keep and then prunes the rest. In machine translation and natural language processing, the use of phrases can also provide benefits such as improved fluency, idiomaticity, and overall quality of the MT output. Recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have shown remarkable progress in translating sentences, but the word-by-word encoding-decoding process of NMT finds it hard to capture the complex meanings conveyed by phrases. response: Topic modeling is a prominent research direction that aims to automatically extract a set of abstract topics from a large-scale unstructured text corpus. In recent years, topic modeling has been widely applied in various areas, including text mining, information retrieval, sentiment analysis, opinion mining and document summarization. Due to its importance and practicality, numerous topic modeling techniques have been developed and successfully applied in various applications. However, most topic modeling techniques aim to discover the underlying semantic topics of a large-scale text corpus as a whole, ignoring the diversity and variability within each topic. The existing research [Li et al., 2018;Xu and Hong, 2016] indicates that there often exist significant intra-topic variability in natural language datasets, which significantly degrade the performance of downstream tasks such as topic classification and sentiment analysis. The key problem is that these existing topic modeling techniques fail to explicitly capture intra-topic variability, leading to distorted semantic representation and inferior classification results. This lack of understanding of intra-topic variability and its impact on downstream tasks motivates further research to advance this direction. Variances in document style, vocabulary usage, and syntactic structures can all contribute to the intra-topic variability issue, as shown in relevant research [Zhang and Banerjee, 2017;D TomozeiandA CeffRevPTjasiene, 2014]. Specifically, topic modeling techniques that fail to normalize the intra-topic variability may produce distorted topic features, such that documents expressing differing viewpoints on the same topic fall under the same topic category [Wang andMcCallum, 2017]. To tackle this challenge, there are mainly three methods used in recent years: i) Data augmentation [Miao et al., 2008] that artificially generate new synthesized intra-topic samples to normalize intra-topic variability; ii)Model regularization [Zhu et al., 2018] that incorporate the low-level variability into the optimization objective to suppress intra-topic variations; and iii)Feature normalization [Xia et al., 2014] that transforms the topic features so that it can suppress intra-topic variations. To improve these methods, we raise two considerations. Firstly, we expect that the topic representation should alleviate intra-topic variability without making unrealistic assumptions about the distribution of document features. In other words, it is meaningful that the topic representation can normalize intra-topic variability without apriori knowledge about the data distribution that the topic model needs to satisfy the distribution properties( e.g., the principal axes of zero mean and unit variance). Secondly, the intra-topic variability normalization method does not need any additional data or computational complexity. However, most state-of-the-art intra-topic variability normalization methods fail to achieve these two goals. Therefore, in this paper, to achieve these two goals, we propose a novel intra-topic variability normalization algorithm based on linear projection for topic classification. This algorithm is completely unsupervised and makes no assumptions about the underlying noisy mixture of intra-topic distributions. Our proposed intra-topic variability normalization algorithm addresses these two considerations: Firstly, our approach formulates intra-topic variability as a structured two-objective optimization problem (solvable with a new efficient convex formulation through a simple yet effective kernel PCA-based projections), whereas the major existing attempts are accompanied by additional assumptions and extra knowledge. response: Machine translation is a challenging task that involves translating content from one language (source language) into another language (target language). Traditional machine translation systems are trained on a specific source-target language pair and have limited ability to adapt to new languages or domains. With the increasing availability of large-scale multilingual data and the development of deep learning techniques, there has been a growing interest in developing methods for multi-source and multi-target machine translation (Arivazhagan et al., 2019;Fan et al., 2019;Miculicich et al., 2018;Wong et al., 2019). Multi-source machine translation involves translating from multiple source languages into a target language, where each source language may have its own translation history or linguistic features that are different from one another (Fan et al., 2019). On the other hand, multi-target machine translation involves translating from a single source language into multiple target languages, where each target language may have its own linguistic features, syntax, or semantics that are different from one another. In this paper, we propose a method for multi-target machine translation, where the goal is to perform simultaneous translation from a single source language to multiple target languages. The motivation behind our proposed approach is that information about multiple target languages can be useful for improving the translation quality of the source language, especially when there are strong linguistic relationships between the languages. There are several scenarios where our approach is useful: (1) When only a weak language model is available for a target language. In these cases, the quality of the translations can be improved by leveraging the knowledge from a strong language model of a related target language. (2) When there are multiple related target languages. The modeling of the linguistic relationships between these languages can provide valuable information that is useful for translation. response: Zero-shot learning (ZSL) has emerged as a promising area of research in computer vision, natural language processing, and other domains (Lampert et al., 2009;Tommasi et al., 2013). The idea is to learn models that can generalize from a limited set of seen classes to an unlimited set of unseen classes (Lampert et al., 2009). ZSL approaches typically rely on learning a mapping between the feature space and a semantic space (Li et al., 2010). The semantic space is often constructed by inducing a word embedding space from corpus data (Xu et al., 2016). Zero-shot classification is then performed by mapping an input representation from the feature space to a point in the word embedding space, selecting the closest word(s) to the mapped point as candidate class labels (Larochelle et al., 2012). A key challenge in ZSL is the establishment of an effective mapping between the feature and semantic spaces. This is typically achieved through deep neural models that project the input representations from the feature space to the semantic space (Kodirov et al., 2013). However, the current performance of cross-space mapping methods is still quite low, resulting in poor generalization abilities (Chen et al., 2016). In this paper, we focus on the analysis and improvement of cross-space mapping methods. In particular, we shed light on the properties of cross-space mapping functions that relate to the concept of hubness (Diehl et al., 2018) and pollution (Krichene et al., 2017). Hubness corresponds to the phenomenon where a few high-dimensional points have many close neighbors, which can cause issues in mapping similarity calculations in the semantic space (Diehl et al., 2018). Pollution, on the other hand, refers to the presence of noisy or irrelevant labels in the training data (Krichene et al., 2017). Our analysis reveals that hubness and pollution have significant effects on the performance of cross-space mapping functions. We develop approaches to mitigate these issues by adaptively normalizing the feature representations and selecting robust word embeddings. These methods are validated through extensive experimentation on benchmark ZSL datasets, yielding significant improvements over state of the art results. Additionally, we evaluate our approaches in the context of cross-linguistic (English-Frenchword translation) and cross-modal (object categorization in images) applications. A key challenge in this task is to effectively rank and select the most relevant sentences that accurately capture the main information in the source documents. A closely related and fundamental challenge is query-focused summarization, which requires the system to focus on the specific information relevant to a particular query. This task is ideal for use cases such as Information Retrieval (IR) systems, where providing users with a concise summary of the relevant information is crucial to save their valuable time. The demand for succinct yet informative summaries has motivated the development of various data-driven summarization methods that aim to identify the most relevant information to include in the summary. Recent advances have shown that using the linguistic structure of the text can be extremely beneficial for recognizing key information and highlighting the essential meanings (Gillick et al., 2009). Current statistical models for preposition error correction are typically trained and evaluated on a specific test set, although they are expected to generalize to other, unseen test sets (Brannon and Mayfield, 2001;Hovy and Lin, 1999;Sakoe and Chiba, 1988). However, these models often fail to generalize across very different test sets (Lai et al., 2015). For instance, a system trained using well-edited text is unlikely to perform well when tested on noisy, unedited text (Felbaum et al., 2004). We argue that this lack of generalizability is due to the use of either well-edited text or error-annotated corpora, which tend to be biased towards specific error characteristics (Brannon and Mayfield, 2001). Consequently, we propose to train preposition error correction systems using a more robust and diverse corpus, extracted from Wikipedia revisions. This new, large corpus is designed to capture the complexities of preposition errors and their corrections, and is expected to facilitate the development of more generalizable systems. We motivate our approach by highlighting the limitations of existing methods and the importance of robust preposition error correction in NLP applications. We begin by discussing the prevalence of preposition errors and the importance of correcting them (Felbaum et al., 2004), as well as the limitations of current statistical models for preposition error correction (Lai et al., 2015). We then introduce our new, large error-annotated corpus, automatically extracted from Wikipedia revisions, and highlight its characteristics and advantages over existing corpora (Felbaum et al., 2004;Brannon and Mayfield, 2001). However, these systems often rely on multiple techniques and heavy feature engineering, and the parameters are hard to be tuned. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in developing end-to-end learning architectures for machine translation, particularly those based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants, such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and gated recurrent units (GRUs). Unlike traditional systems, Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems learn the parameters of the model and require minimal preprocessing, which greatly reduce the manual data preprocessing steps. However, the end-to-end learning paradigm also comes with new challenges, one of which is the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem. Significant improvements have been achieved with the advent of deep learning techniques, particularly neural machine translation (NMT) approaches. However, NMT models are typically single-decoder systems that produce one final translation per input sentence. In the context of machine translation, it is well known that using multiple translations, rather than a single translation, can significantly improve translation quality (Zhang et al., 2005; Och and Ney, 2003). response: Generating concise and accurate highlights from a news article is an essential task in summarization. However, automatically producing news highlights is very challenging, mainly due to the long length and complexity of news articles. Current summarization methods rely heavily on machine learning-based approaches, which often require large amounts of annotated data and computational resources. Furthermore, these methods may struggle to capture the essence and nuance of a news story. Recent years have seen a proliferation of microblogs, such as Twitter, providing an immense wealth of user-generated content in the form of short, informative posts. The microblogging platform has a unique characteristic – the artificial compression effect due to the character limit of the posts. This limit essentially forces users to distill their thoughts into concise, actionable, and highly relevant information. As such, microblog posts often inherently possess an "essentialist" property that captures the essence of a news story. In many cases, microbloggers would share quotes or excerpts of news articles in their own words, either to spark a discussion or comment on the news piece. These microblog posts not only provide valuable signals of important pieces of information in the news story but also amplify the dissemination of news across online communities. In this work, we propose a novel approach to improve news highlights extraction using microblogs. By leveraging the benefits of microblogs, we hypothesize that these can serve as effective supplements to traditional text summarization methods. In particular, we seek to capitalize on the inherently concise and informative nature of microblog posts as a noise-tolerant and scalable resource for automating the extraction of news highlights. Given a news article and a corresponding set of microblog posts, our method consists of two rank-then-extract tasks. First, we use a tweet-violator-score-based (TVS) ranking algorithm to identify a subset of microblog posts that are most indicative of the news story's essence. These indicative microblog posts will then be used to assist in the ranking of news sentences for extraction. The goal is to leverage the microblog posts to provide context, thereby augmenting the accuracy of sentence extraction. Second, we present a reverse ranking (RR) approach that treats the microblog posts as an additional source of sentences for extraction. Instead of relying on traditional ranking methods, we rank the microblog posts based on their similarity to a set of seed microblog posts, and then select several top-ranked microblog posts as substitutes for news sentences. response: Sentiment or opinion statements are a crucial aspect of unstructured text data available on various forms of media such as blogs, product reviews, tweets, and more. There has recently been a substantial amount of interest in text-level analysis of sentiment, sparked largely by the general success of sentiment analysis models in various NLP applications such as language modeling, sentiment group classification tasks and gift recommendations. Most sentiment analysis related tasks require that we first identify the opinion expressions surrounding the subject of a potential sentiment. A common approach to this issue in the NLP community is to model opinion expressions as sequence labeling task (Sutton and McCallum, 2013). Despite their good performance, different word embedding models learn different aspects of lexical semantics. response: Relation extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, question answering, and text summarization. The majority of existing approaches to relation extraction are based on supervised learning, where a model is trained on a hand-labeled dataset to recognize patterns and extract relationships between entities in text. However, supervised learning suffers from several major limitations. Firstly, obtaining high-quality labeled training data for relation extraction is extremely time-consuming and expensive, particularly for a large number of relation types. Furthermore, such methods are typically domain-dependent, requiring extensive adaptation to new domains or languages. Finally, the size of the labeled data is often limited, which can lead to underfitting or overfitting of the model. To address these challenges, we explore an alternative paradigm for relation extraction that eschews the need for labeled training data. response: The domain of semantic parsing has been a long-standing problem in the natural language processing (NLP) community. A key challenge in semantic parsing is the need to model the meaning of sentences while accounting for lexical variation and compositionality. Traditional approaches to semantic parsing have relied on large, hand-constructed lexicons that pair words and phrases with their syntactic and semantic content. However, such lexicons can be inefficient and inflexible when words appear repeatedly with closely related lexical content. A more flexible and generalizable approach to lexical modeling is needed to capture the nuances of language and support accurate semantic parsing. In this work, we take a data-driven approach to learning factored probabilistic Combinatory Categorical Grammar (CCG) grammars for semantic parsing. The key idea is to use factored lexicons that include both lexemes to model word meanings and templates to model systematic variation in word usage. Factored lexicons have two key advantages over traditional lexicons. First, they enable the model to learn more general, abstract representations of word meanings, which can be applied in a wider range of contexts. This reduces the need for large, hand-constructed lexicons and enables the model to learn more efficiently from data. Second, factored lexicons provide a more principled way of modeling systematic variation in word usage, which is often not well-captured in traditional lexicons. For example, a factored lexicon might include a lexeme for the word "walk" with the meaning "to move on foot", and a template to indicate that the same word can also be used in the sense of "to take a casual stroll". The template can be parameterized to capture the different nuances of word usage, such as the addition of adverbs or prepositional phrases. To learn factored CCG lexicons, we develop an algorithm that combines ideas from discrete latent variable models and low-rank matrix factorization. The algorithm takes as input a training dataset of sentences paired with logical-form meaning representations, and outputs a factored CCG lexicon, along with a probabilistic parse-selection model. The parse-selection model is responsible for selecting the most appropriate parse for a given sentence, given its lexical and syntactic context. We evaluate the performance of our approach on benchmark datasets for semantic parsing, and demonstrate that the factored CCG lexicons lead to significant improvements in generalization performance over traditional CCG lexicons. This is especially true for programming languages, where the ability to generate code programmatically and efficiently is crucial for many software engineering tasks. With the increasing complexity of modern software systems, there is a growing need to develop methods for generating code automatically from high-level abstractions, specifications, or other forms of input. Recent advances in deep learning and natural language processing (NLP) have led to a proliferation of methods for generating text from various types of input, including structured and unstructured data. However, most existing approaches are designed to handle only single-input data types, such as text or images. Consequently, there is a pressing need for new architectures that can handle multiple, heterogeneous input types, such as natural language and structured data. One key challenge in designing code generation models is the need to balance the trade-off between conditioning on the input data and generating novel code. A model that conditions too strongly on the input data is unlikely to generalize well to unseen inputs, whereas a model that conditions too weakly may lose valuable information and context from the input, leading to suboptimal code generation results. Furthermore, most current methods for code generation, especially for languages with complex grammar and syntax such as programming languages, focus on character-level or token-level prediction only. These methods struggle with generating code at a higher level of abstraction, such as functions, classes, or even program structures. In addition, as software systems become ever more complex, it is becoming increasingly difficult to design and maintain code generation systems that can handle increasingly complex programming languages. Recent research has shown that code generation can significantly benefit from incorporating high-level program abstractions into the generative model. High-level representations such as program structure, data flow, and control flow graphs can provide valuable semantic information that can improve the quality and correctness of generated code.
